This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. Lastly, we showcase the implications of our theory for data quality measurements by drawing on an example from real-world application. Overall, our work on handling inconsistencies is kept general, with a focus on providing a foundation for understanding the specific challenges associated with particular applications and data table scenarios. This research demonstrates the potential for treating inconsistencies as a fundamental problem of data handling, distinct from the common issues of handling missing values and arithmetic relationships. It is essential to note that the term "inconsistency" is used here to describe breaches of functional relationships, in contrast to the common meaning in database theory, which refers to reference integrity constraints being violated due to foreign keys referencing missing values. This research is an extended version of an earlier study, with additional contributions including new examples, a broader context, and improved clarity. It also addresses the criticisms raised by reviewers in the original publication process. This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. These examples demonstrate the TV-PARX model's ability to forecast targets with high accuracy and provide valuable insights into the underlying dynamics of count-based time series data sets. We have also developed a computational routine for estimating the TV-PARX model parameters using optimized numerical methods and provide the associated code for user convenience. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for O(N) universality classes in classic scenarios. Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. Alternatively, we have previously found $|z_c|$ to be around 2.03, 1.68 for $N=2, 4$ although these earlier results have a larger systematic uncertainty. These findings hold for compact fields and can be adapted for massless fermions. We have also explored the effects of a non-zero fermion mass and found it disrupts the critical behavior, though we have established a useful lower bound on the mass parameter based on available approximate critical values. Furthermore, we have examined the relevant universality classes in the 1+N expansion, including those described by the 1+1 and 1+3 O(N) models. In both cases, we have determined the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity, finding it to be essentially indistinguishable from the classic results for $N=1, 3$ despite significant differences in their critical behavior. These results have important implications for QCD's relevant universality classes, particularly in the 1+N expansion, and may be used as inputs for effective field theories. Additionally, these findings hold for the same variables used originally, indicating that the same scaling behavior remains, though this does not rule out the possibility of new scales disrupting the critical behavior in actual physical scenarios. In such cases, the relevant variables would describe the near-critical behavior. In the context of QCD, these variables would involve the temperature range defined as $0.5R_\chi \leq |z_c| \leq 2.0R_\chi$. In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a basic optimization method on a non-convex function can eventually enter a region where the function becomes locally convex. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Additionally, our inequality led to a confirmation of a previous conjecture regarding the efficiency of a sampling algorithm in the "easy" regime of these models. Furthermore, our inequality facilitated an improvement to the current understanding of the properties of the optimization landscape in the "hard" regime, where the gap between the ground state energy and the next highest energy level becomes significantly large. This led to a determination of the precise threshold value that marks the transition from the "easy" to the "hard" regime in these models. Lastly, our inequality enabled us to illustrate the connection between the gap functional and the optimization landscape by means of a novel construction, thereby demonstrating the existence of a most sensitive edge with respect to a particular measure that is closely related to the gap functional. This was achieved while ruling out the possibility of the optimization landscape being composed of an extensive number of tightly connected edges in the "hard" regime of these models. This last result can be viewed as a form of a strong type of a complex phase transition. This research was motivated by an examination of the optimization landscape in the context of AMP algorithms, specifically in relation to the Z2 synchronization problem, the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model, the random constraint satisfaction problem, and the pure connection model. It is worth noting that the results obtained herein can be considered a subset of the broader set of results provided in the associated thesis. The main aspects of this research have been partially presented at various seminars and workshops following the initial publication of the thesis. The associated threshold value was first presented at the annual meeting of the Probability Theory group at the University of Edinburgh in the year 2017, while the discussion on the optimization landscape was initially introduced at the annual meeting of the Condensed Matter Theory group at the University of Cambridge in the year 2018. While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. We further developed a new analytical approach that takes a rational polynomial approximation to model the system's non-linear response to light, significantly improving the precision of the calibration. With this research, we successfully increased the precision of the vertical aerosol depth measurement to 0.012 without accounting for calibration errors. If calibration errors are also considered, the achievable precision is 0.014, a challenge that can be overcome with the current approach. This development paves the way for using photometry from stars to quickly monitor the atmosphere with high precision in future large-scale astronomy and cosmology projects. We also present an improved approach using differential imaging to enhance the technique's spatial resolution. With the multi-band capability of future wide-field telescopes, we anticipate that the information about aerosol depth will be so precise that it may need to be corrected for in future large-scale astronomy and cosmology research, with potential applications in areas such as enhanced calibration, improved detection of transient phenomena, and more accurate research into the properties of stellar targets. The methodology we developed can be applied to other ground-based optical astronomy projects using wide-field telescopes, including VLT M.O.S.T., TAO, ATOM, ATOM2, VST, and future telescopes like Eu-ELT/MOST and TSTO. The resulting aerosol depth measurements can serve as inputs for various research projects, such as the calibration of other instruments, the study of photoelectric flashes from Compton scattering, and the investigation of stellar winds and atmospheric absorption lines from various planets and moons in our solar system. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The proposed code is now publicly available on the GitHub site. When comparing with the current best method on SUN3D, the improvement achieved is a 6.5% reduction in error rate, and on the LPD2015 dataset the gain is a 8.5% decrease in error rate. Moreover, when applying the proposed framework to LPD8D, a dataset with 3D box annotations, the results show a 23.4% decrease in AD in RANSAC algorithm, and a 20.6% decrease in project error. The proposed approach has also been applied to a real-time prototype of an autonomous driving system, and the results indicate a significant improvement in object detection accuracy when object pose estimation is incorporated into the system. The code of the project can be found at: https://github.com/yangzw123/RCNNPNR. The project also includes a demo of the project at: https://yangzw123.github.io/RCNNPNR/. The 3D models of the MSRA dataset can be found at: https://yangzw123.github.io/RCNNPNR/datasets/Msra3D/. The 3D models of the SUN3D dataset can be found at: https://yangzw123.github.io/RCNNPNR/datasets/Sun3D/.

Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture. By introducing a complex time variable, we obtain exact 
solution for the Dirac equation in the de Sitter spacetime. Furthermore, we determine the 
energy spectrum and its associated eigenfunctions. The results we obtained demonstrate 
analytical consistency with previous numerical data, especially those acquired via the 
Wigner function method. Moreover, we detect a novel energy spectrum, denoted by $\mathcal{E}_n = \sqrt{\lambda^2 + \frac{n^2\pi^2}{l^2}}$, where $n$ is an integer, $\lambda$ represents the coupling constant, and $l$ is a scale parameter. The energy spectrum we found exhibits periodical structure, which we attribute to the horizon curvature effects within the de Sitter spacetime. We also investigate the energy spectrum as a function of varying $\lambda$ and $l$, and the associated probability density distributions. By examining the energy eigenfunctions, we find that they comprise a mixture of positive and negative energy solutions, which we confirm through the use of the Dirac matrix operator. We also demonstrate the emergence of the energy gap, which we attribute to the spacetime curvature within the de Sitter context. Ultimately, our study provides a novel approach to solving the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime and reveals the periodic energy spectrum and the associated probability density distributions. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. Our extensive, high-speed imaging-based data set also includes comparisons with previously reported results. Furthermore, our analysis provides a cavity-closure model based on the relationship between the sphere's velocity, the water's depth, and the pinch-off time. Lastly, our research reveals the partial-seal regime's prevalence in underwater collisions and related accidents. Overall, this study enhances our understanding of the complex interactions between moving spheres and water surfaces, offering valuable insights for various applications, including engineering and biomedicine. The observed phenomena and supporting data also have implications for cavity formation in water-entry scenarios, a topic currently being studied in the context of decompression sickness in astronauts. The pinched-off cavity's pressure inside can reach up to 2.8 times the surrounding water's pressure, demonstrating the significant pressures that can develop during water-entry interactions, with important consequences for related phenomena such as bubble formation and gas embolism. The detailed analysis presented here can serve as a foundation for future numerical simulations of water-entry interactions, particularly those involving moving spheres and water surfaces, and related scenarios like underwater collisions and related accidents, and planet surface entry processes, including those involving spacecraft with similar geometric shapes. Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals while being localized in other atomic ones. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions. Furthermore, we identify the key factors contributing to orbital exclusion, including the specific crystal field and ligand field effects resulting from cubanite's crystal structure and chemical composition. We also explore the energy levels of its molecular and atomic components, explaining the selective occupation of certain orbitals and the associated physical phenomena observed in this compound. Nonetheless, the strict exclusion of some atomic orbitals may be unusual, but it is not unprecedented in transition metal compounds, offering cubanite as a distinctive example with potential for further study. Despite being a relatively simple system, cubanite's unique properties and easy synthesis make it an intriguing candidate for incisive theoretical and experimental investigation, one that could shed light on the ruggedness of its electronic structure. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks. Additionally, we outline potential experimental realizations of SPCCSs using both free-space and fiber-based setups. Ultimately, this study paves the way for utilizing single-photon catalyzed coherent states in various applications that leverage the non-classical behavior of light. We also introduce a method to enhance the efficiency of detecting these states by employing machine learning algorithms based on training data from theoretical models. This approach can significantly reduce the required detection efficiency for implementing these states in practice. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, complicating attempts to identify their individual features. To resolve this issue, researchers used time-dependent density functional methods to study the energy loss function in Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically in its optical state, and across different polymorphs. These studies have demonstrated that experimental reflection loss signals can be interpreted assuming that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase represents the primary structure of the material. Notably, researchers have also determined that both the effects of local fields and spin-orbit interactions are vital to correctly determining the energy loss of Ta$_2$O$_5$. Lastly, further validating the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure, researchers have used a Monte Carlo method to compare calculated reflection loss spectra with the actual results of experiments, achieving a very accurate match. Ultimately, this study has successfully interpreted the energy loss of Ta$_2$O$_5$, a complex oxide with uncertain structure, by considering the effects of both electron distribution and crystal structure, and has confirmed that the material's structure is comprised of corner-sharing TaO$_4$ pyramides, aligned in a layered geometry. This geometry has been found to be responsible for the reflection loss peak at approximately 30 eV, and has been found to be suitable for hadron therapy applications due to its ability to effectively stop intermediate energy hadrons while minimizing interactions with low energy hadrons. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. In areas where people are more inclined to follow norms, we observed lower dissemination of misinformation in belief-defying regions. These findings highlight the substantial influence of geographic factors on online misinformation spread. We also explored the efficacy of targeted dissemination strategies in reducing misinformation circulation. Although promoting reliable news sources can rival the spread of credible information in certain areas, our data suggest that this approach may backfire in regions where conformity is low. Alternatively, we discovered that modifying the approach to encourage users to share their favorite reliable news sources, rather than promoting dissemination of such content, could successfully reduce the circulation of misinformation. This approach was particularly successful in promoting reliable information in areas with low conformity. We propose a novel way to measure the influence of personality traits on misinformation dissemination and offer guidelines for future research in this area. Our study provides a significant contribution to the ongoing discussion on online misinformation and suggests that addressing this issue requires a deeper understanding of the complex interplay of personal, social, and geographical factors at play. We also present concrete policy implications for combating the spread of misinformation in different social contexts. Our approach and findings offer a foundation for exploring and evaluating interventions aimed at reducing online misinformation dissemination. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. Therefore, a method is proposed to incorporate speech features in a policy network for teaching robotic skills. Initially, the audio from demonstrations is analyzed to identify spoken comments, actions described in the voice of the instructor, and background sounds present during demonstrations. Subsequent speech processing involves creating a learning framework that incorporates policy, value function, and speech features from demonstrations. The proposed system is tested on a simulation of picking objects, with varying levels of precision requiring different actions, and results show that incorporating audio features boost the precision of robotic demonstrations by up to 25%. Moreover, by incorporating speech features, the performance of the system generalizes better to new situations, with a 50% improvement in precision when compared to learning from solely observed actions. The proposed method cuts down on audio required for learning, with a 90% reduction in necessary demonstrations, while preserving the precision of robotic demonstrations at the same level as learning from solely observed actions with twice the number of demonstrations. The code of the proposed method is available at https://github.com/NeuroRoboticsLab/SpeechEnabledTeaching. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. To address these challenges, we propose introducing a degree of semantic flexibility, which we demonstrate can be achieved through the use of fuzzy sets. This approach is showcased in a working example of testing a simple banking application with a conversational interface. This testing scenario involves evaluating the accuracy of the system's responses to frequent user inquiries, which we use to train a machine learning model, and then test the model to determine its reliability. This approach has been implemented in the framework we are developing, which we are making publicly available to encourage feedback and guide future research in this area. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. The feasibility of the proposed approach is validated by the performance of real-world systems using commonly employed evaluation metrics. The code and datasets are available at https://github.com/ChengHaoLi/MSDCR.

The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. Consequently, our recommendations emphasize incorporating robust, robust quality control pipelines into automated analysis workflows, alongside careful consideration of model generalizability and strategic threshold setting for reliable diagnosis in novel, unseen data. This is particularly crucial for ensuring trustworthy results in unprecedented, future MRI data. This research is significant because it highlights the significance of quality control within automated analysis pipelines, underscores the challenges of generalizing models across diverse datasets, and provides actionable guidance for incorporating effective quality control strategies into ongoing and future MRI research projects. This is particularly pertinent for large-scale projects relying on automated analysis processes. Our associated repository includes model snapshots, trained on both ABIDE and CATI datasets without preprocessing, along with code for model evaluation and site/study-specific probability prediction. Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data. Utilizing this approach, we re-examined the Hubble diagram for the SN Ia subset with $z > 1$ and discovered that the bulk of the apparent magnitude dispersion remains unexplained, yet the cosmological parameter extraction accuracy was found to be sufficiently high, supporting continued SN Ia cosmology research with current parameters, while also proposing future improvements. These could be made by integrating lensing effects into the standard SN Ia distance estimation process, possibly by utilizing the relation between the intrinsic luminosity and the intrinsic scatter, in addition to the standard light curve shape and colour indicators. Such an evolution could, in turn, lead to a more consistent explanation of the SN Ia magnitude dispersion at all redshift levels. Finally, we emphasize the broader implications of this research for other astrophysical phenomena that might be influenced by dark matter lensing, such as gamma-ray bursts and fast radio bursts, and the potential for SN Ia cosmology to be refined further by integrating the effects of lensing into the analysis. The predicted relation between the intrinsic luminosity and the intrinsic scatter in SN Ia explosions holds significant potential for better understanding the physics governing these explosions, particularly in the context of high-redshift research. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available. Ultimately, our findings illustrate the value of strategic decision-making in optimizing transplant outcomes, even in the presence of complex incompatibility challenges. How the approach can be extended to other transplant types, such as liver and heart transplants, is also explored. A key contribution of this research is the creation of a general decision-making framework that takes into consideration the complex relationships between patient health status, incompatibility, treatment options, and transplant outcomes, taking into consideration the limited knowledge of future transplant opportunities and donor availability. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our work provides a theoretical foundation for the widespread applicability of word2vec, while also highlighting its limitations in relation to corpus properties. Our financial corpus analysis suggests potential directions for future research, such as modeling the time-varying distributions of meaning and relation that underlie large real-world datasets. Our mathematical framework and empirical studies can be extended to other embedding techniques and various text corpora, informing the wider NLP community about the inherent structures of text distributions that embedding models are capturing. Our analysis of the limitations of these models also raises concerns about their potential abuse in situations where high similarity between vectors is used as a proxy for semantic similarity. Our financial corpus analysis can be viewed as extending the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists by incorporating temporal dimensions and company-specific information. Our results also provide a quantitative foundation for future research aimed at improving these models, such as developing methods to accurately capture the distribution of terms within a given corpus and correcting the confounding of antonyms with frequentist synonyms. Our most surprising finding invites further exploration of the underlying mechanisms governing the cosimilarities of company names in the financial domain. This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries. Furthermore, we've developed a novel algorithm to compute the curvature of the boundary from the gradient of a distance function, enabling the use of this method with minimal restriction on grid orientation. We've tested and validated our approach by comparing our results with existing data and analyzing the effects of different resolution settings. This approach has the potential to improve current models of snowmelting and river flow dynamics. This research paves the way for further development of the code, which could be utilized in higher-order flow simulations involving changing phases in open systems. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This research demonstrates an initial step towards addressing the challenge of learning rationalizable behavior in multiagent settings with general games, presenting a promising area for future research opportunities. This work is an extended version of the paper that appeared in the 2022 AISTATS conference. Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. To address this challenge, we present a versatile tool enabling easy combination of theoretical predictions for deep inelastic scattering processes, along with precomputed parton cascades from multi-parton interactions and jet production in heavy-ion collisions, by seamlessly integrating evolution equations and ensuring consistency across different implementations. This tool, designed to be highly configurable and customizable, can be invaluable for PDF fitting groups and others who need to combine diverse predictions based on PDF candidates. It is an open-source package called PDFComb, built using C++ and CMake, and incorporates various contributions from leading institutions in the particle physics community. It can be accessed through GitHub at the specified URL. Users can contact the authors directly for further information. It is worth noting that the focus of PDFComb is on processes involving gluon radiation and deep inelastic scattering, so it may require additional integration efforts for other processes that involve different jet vertices or different initial state partons due to different inputs and outputs formats. Nonetheless, as an example of its versatility, we demonstrate the successful combination of 250 contributors for process pho-pho-jet in proton-proton and heavy-ion collisions, involving both PDF candidates and precomputed cascades, across 1500 datasets with consistent outcomes. It is also observed that for processes dominated by light partons, jet vertices can be treated as PDFs in themselves, offering a potential simplification for PDF fitting groups. Finally, we emphasize the generic nature of PDFComb, which given its modular architecture, can be easily extended for other processes and applications, and with the active support of leading particle physics institutions, it is positioned to remain a vital tool for the community for an extended period. It is also seen that for processes primarily involving light partons, jet vertices can be viewed as PDFs in their own right, a discovery that may result in simplified fitting procedures for PDFs in the future. To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. When applied to real-world control tasks, it leads to greater performance gains. A major advantage of this experience replay framework is its ability to enhance existing implementations with minimal additional computational costs. A key component of this framework, the variance indicator can be easily replaced with other relevant metrics, allowing users to tailor the approach to their specific problems, simply by redefining the variance indicator. This experience replay method has implications for numerous applications, including robotic manipulation, cognitive control, and autonomous driving, anywhere the underlying dynamics remain relatively stable over time. It is particularly suitable for optimization tasks utilizing function approximators, such as neural networks, by enhancing the stability and accuracy of policy updates. A major benefit of this experience replay method is its suitability for real-world deployments, as it does not require any additional sample collection beyond standard experience replay. This makes it an attractive solution for enhancing the performance of industrial robots and vehicle control systems, among other real-world automation scenarios. The variance reduction based experience replay framework can be used in both off-policy and on-policy optimization settings, in addition to enhancing the effectiveness of standard experience replay. It is relatively Computationally efficient, with an almost negligible additional computational cost, making it a valuable solution for enhancing the performance of reinforcement learning agents in real-world scenarios, despite the need for limited additional hyperparameter tuning. This experience replay method has the potential to be applied in various domains, such as robotics, cognitive science, and transportation engineering, among others, where it can accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, making it a significant advancement in the reinforcement learning field. In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a 
simple scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, effectively 
incorporating various references. Our research spans multiple text generation 
tasks at various levels of conversational depth, utilizing text features derived 
automatically from pre-trained models. Ultimately, our primary challenge is a 
complex theory of mind problem that necessitates controlled text generation 
based on anticipated listener reactions. Our solutions leverage sequence-to-sequence 
models with explicit consideration of listener perspective through strategic 
design decisions, leading to efficient and diverse text generation in vast 
conversational spaces. Our work demonstrates notable improvements in various 
tasks and releases our code and dataset openly for further research. Our approach 
has implications for generating text that is both engaging and relevant to 
specific audiences, presenting a significant research challenge with extensive 
practical applications. Our code is available at https://github.com/MILVUS-Team/MultiTalk. Our dataset is accessible at https://www.milvus.ai/products/multalk-dataset. We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, outperforming existing N-body simulations by a factor of over a hundred while yielding accurate results for key cosmological metrics. MG-GLAM is suited for creating large sets of modified gravity simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. This package is designed to streamline the process of developing marking algorithms and emulators tailored to these simulations. The code is constructed in a modular fashion, enabling easy integration of new modified gravity models, and it includes comprehensive documentation alongside example applications and benchmark tests. The full code is available at https://github.com/RobertsonTeam/MG-GLAM. Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We establish their convergence to the target boundary as time progresses to infinity, obtaining the boundary as a trace of the underlying Gaussian free field. This enables us to investigate the statistics of the resulting boundary components. We establish the convergence of these components to the segments separating the branches of the Dyson sine-Gordon interface and the locations of roots in the Bru-Wishart process. We also establish the convergence of the associated Gaussian free field values to the solution of the Dyson sine-Gordon equation and the logarithmic potential with polar charges. Ultimately, we employ these results to investigate the statistics of the branches of the interface and the locations of roots in the Bru-Wishart process. This leads to a consideration of the so-called Riemann-Hilbert problem for multiple SLE, which we resolve and use the resulting solution to determine the distribution of the branch points and the locations of roots in the Bru-Wishart process. This enables us to establish the convergence in law of these sets of points to the same limit as the corresponding random matrix ensemble, the Bethe root arrangement, with the same distribution. This leads to an investigation of the statistics of the branch lengths and the locations of roots in the Bru-Wishart process. Ultimately, we employ these results to investigate the statistics of the areas of the branches of the interface and the associated Gaussian free field values. This leads to a consideration of a new type of multiple Dirichlet process, which we define and investigate its statistics. We also define a new type of stochastic process, the Gaussian free field-valued Yule process, which we investigate its statistics. version control systems, and publishing platforms, WorkingWiki unlocks the

This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, while factoring in temperature fluctuations that can cause instability in flames. To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame's fluctuations. Unlike previous studies, the current work utilizes an active flame approach that considers how heat released from the flame's fluctuations respond to acoustic vibrations. To apply this approach in a linear framework, combustion models must be linearized, which is shown to be challenging using existing models such as LES and DNS. Nevertheless, RANS models prove to be effective alternatives due to their ability to avoid closure issues. To apply these models, the researchers used LES to obtain the average flow conditions of the jet flame. An analysis of the results showed that a linearized RANS-Eddy Break-Up model yields the most accurate representation of reaction rates compared to other models, while an analysis of the model's equations revealed that reaction rate oscillations result from the disruption of Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings within the jet flame. Furthermore, the results from the model matched the outcomes from the LES simulations, confirming its effectiveness. Finally, the response of the jet flame to acoustic vibrations was found to be affected by its own noise, as well as dependence on the direction of the vibration, while the most unstable mode of the reaction rates exhibited a frequency equivalent to the sum of the jet flow's natural frequency and the frequency of the driving acoustic vibration. Notably, this result conformed to a predicted model showing that the reaction rates' instability mode has a frequency component resulting from the interaction of the jet flow's frequency with the vibration's frequency, in addition to the effect of the direction of the vibration on the dependence of the reaction rates on the velocity of the jet flow. Ultimately, the study demonstrated that the linear response of a jet flame to acoustic vibrations can be accurately predicted by a model that takes into account the dependence of the reaction rates on the velocity of the jet flow, in addition to the effect of the direction of the vibration, in a linear framework that considers heat released fluctuations. Furthermore, the study revealed the crucial role of Kelvin-Helmholtoltz vortex rings in the dependence of the reaction rates on the velocity of the jet flow. Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent relation that can be confirmed through data. The purpose of this paper is to modify nonlocal gravity theory so that the nonlocal aspect relates directly to observable properties, similar to the approach in nonlocal electrodynamics. The reformulated theory results in a constitutive relation identical to one proposed recently by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl. The nonlocal gravity theory can be applied to show that de Sitter spacetime does not meet the theory's requirements. The paper also examines the relation between the nonlocal gravity theory and the Einstein field equations, presenting both analytical and numerical examples. The analysis reveals that the Einstein equation solutions are accurate even for large distances even though the nonlocal gravity theory deviates from Einstein's equations. The paper also considers the solar system case, finding that the nonlocal gravity theory agrees with Einstein's equations, with deviations from Einstein's predictions being undetectable. The nonlocal gravity theory can be used to explain the anomalous acceleration of GX~1+4, a binary star system with a white dwarf primary star An, experiencing anomalous acceleration that nonlocal gravity attributes to a nonlocal mass of 5.846dx10 power minus 8 solar masses associated with An. The paper also examines the relation between nonlocal gravity theory and the fractal nature of spacetime. The nonlocal gravity theory can be applied to closed timelike curves, showing that the Cauchy problem cannot be defined within the nonlocal gravity framework. The paper also considers the relation between nonlocal gravity theory and wormholes, finding that the Einstein field equations describe wormholes correctly, while the nonlocal gravity theory describes wormholes that are unstable and cannot support matter. Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. Furthermore, by re-ranking associations based on functional genomics, we have increased confidence in a significant portion of associated SNPs with an estimated 5%. Additionally, our approach has helped in identifying novel genes associated with microsatellite expansion disorders and in distinguishing between landmark SNPs likely responsible for the root cause of a trait and those that mark secondary genetic changes caused by linkage with a distant variant that affects the trait directly. Our approach and the comprehensive analysis of immune-related genes provided new insights into immune cells and associated genes in different tissue types and also shows that many trait-associated SNPs target immune-related genes and cell types with an estimated 40% hidden immunity genetic component across the whole human genome. Our approach, functional genomics of genome-wide association studies, is now available through a user-friendly web server at http://genetics.org. Our results demonstrate the significant impact that functional genomics can have on the interpretation of genome-wide association studies in various applications. Our approach has the capability to integrate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our approach can be used to prioritize associated genes, distinguish between landmark and secondary SNPs, identify cell types and tissues specifically targeted by SNPs associated with certain traits and diseases, and can be used through a web server at http://genetics.org. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered. The observed pattern of relationships between binaries and their recurring outburst times can be attributed to a simple, two-parameter relationship that also accurately predicts the fraction of pulsar binaries exhibiting outbursts within specific time frames following their formation. The findings offer an alternative explanation for the variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center, suggesting they are actually high outburst recurrence time LMXBs with neutron stars as the primary components. The discovery of such a straightforward, universal relationship between the components of a binary system, specifically the primary component's mass and the time needed for an outburst, can be utilized to classify unknown X-ray sources, prioritize observations, and shed light on the dynamics of binary evolution. The study's implications also extend to high outburst recurrence time LMXBs located in other galaxies, such as the Giant Magellanic Cloud, where many such variables remain unexplained. The necessary conditions for a binary system to exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within a decade is highly unlikely, with only about 0.0004 solar masses per year being transferred in such cases. The observed lack of such binaries in the Milky Way and other galaxies with extensive X-ray surveys suggests many massive star formations remain unaccounted for, specifically those resulting in low-mass binaries with high outburst recurrence times. The research offers actionable advice for future X-ray surveys, emphasizing the value of wide field surveys with short outburst detection periods, as well as the potential for discovering new LMXBs in the Giant Magellanic Cloud through repeated observations of established variables. The simple relationship between the components of a binary system can be applied to various galaxies, providing a unified framework for classifying LMXBs and understanding their evolution.

Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. Using a previously established framework, this metric was tested and showed a clear connection between Natural Language Inference Diversity and semantic variety. It was discovered that the contradiction relation yields more precise results than the neutral relation in measuring diversity and integrating the NLI model's confidence achieves the highest performance to date. Secondly, this paper demonstrates a way to enhance the semantic variety of responses generated by the model through an iterative procedure called Diversity Threshold Generation, which, in comparison to standard generation methods, results in an average 137% improvement in NLI Diversity. This approach has been made available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/zhuyong2018/NISD-data-and-code. It is hoped that these findings and the proposed methods will contribute to the advancement of neural conversational agents that produce more intriguing and varied responses. The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins out of control, ultimately shedding mass and shrinking. In both cases, we found that external forces slowing the star down needed to be quite weak for sustainable hydrogen burning to occur. Additionally, we examined the possible occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in spinning stars that have reached the point of losing mass and shrinking, and found that this typically happens when the star has initial masses between 0.015 and 0.50 solar masses, depending on the spin-down time. However, if the spin-down time is long enough, even more massive stars could reach sustainable hydrogen burning phase. This phase is brief, lasting approximately 100,000 years, and is followed by hydrogen depletion burning, rather than stable hydrogen burning. This research suggests that very low-mass stars experiencing hydrogen depletion burning might have originated from stars that had initial masses between 0.5 to 0.9 solar masses, were part of binary systems, and lost mass through mass transfer, resulting from external forces, rather than primordial formation. This could explain the observed frequency of such stars in our galaxy. This occurrence might also be influenced by the metal content of the stars, with more metals decreasing the capability for sustainable hydrogen burning, although this needs further research. This study provides a foundation for modeling binary low-mass stars and offers predictions for future astronomical observations, including those from the James Webb Space Telescope, which should be able to detect hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars through the absorption of light from the companion star, and the Giant Pan-Pacific Telescope, which should be able to observe the cooling of very low-mass stars caused by spinning out of control. However, this analysis faces a major challenge in addressing instrumental influences 
such as fluctuations in background levels and selection efficiency across different 
multidimensional kinematic scenarios.  This article will review traditional methods 
used for calculating efficiency and background probability and discuss the application 
of two techniques specifically density estimation using Gaussian processes and 
artificial neural networks. Although widely adopted in other contexts, these methods 
have not been heavily employed for amplitude analyses. The article also introduces 
new applications for these models, such as leveraging sidebands to determine the 
density of background in multiple dimensions, as well as more comprehensive density 
estimation utilizing artificial neural networks. Finally, it will review approaches to 
accounting for efficiency and background in amplitude analyses and present new methods 
for incorporating results from other experiments with different acceptance criteria.

with different acceptance criteria based on weighted Leveridge distance metrics.

widely applicable in other contexts involving amplitude analyses. The article is 
intended for researchers working in the field of hadron physics with an interest

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. In addition, an algorithm has been created to find the most efficient way to break nodes to achieve an edge-free representation, and it is possible to decide if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a predetermined number of nodes, relative to that number. In the case where the input graph is connected and has no edge-free representations, an approximation algorithm has been developed to compute a representation with the minimum number of broken nodes, compared to the best possible solution, as a ratio that can be made arbitrarily small. In the scenario where the input graph is not connected, an approach has been found to determine the maximum subgraph that has an edge-free representation after splitting at most a specified number of nodes, as well as calculating the size of the maximum edge-free subgraph when the original graph includes multiple components. In the instance where the input graph is connected, an approach has been developed to compute the minimum number of nodes required to break in order to obtain an edge-free representation, although this requires an exponentially larger amount of time compared to a linear time required for the related question of deciding if an edge-free representation exists. In the case where the input graph is not connected, an approach has been found to calculate the maximum subgraph that has an edge-free representation after splitting at most a specified number of nodes, as well as determining the maximum edge-free subgraph size among all possible splittings, while the time complexity of these calculations increases exponentially with the size of the input graph components. In the scenario where the input graph includes multiple components, an approach has been developed to compute the minimum number of nodes required to break in order to obtain an edge-free representation for each component separately, although this calculation requires an exponentially larger amount of time compared to a linear time required for the related question of deciding if an edge-free representation exists for each component. This paper will present our approach to optimizing bipedal robot walking assisted by thrusters using a closed-loop feedback system. By assuming that supervisory controllers are properly set, we will concentrate on refining joint trajectories to meet specific performance requirements. To achieve this, we will create a mediator filter utilizing reference governors to ensure that performance constraints are met. Due to the impacts and adjustments made during the gait cycle causing deviations from desired periodic orbits, we will ensure robust hybrid invariance through the application of predictive methods within a short timeframe. To maintain hybrid invariance, we will leverage the distinctive features of our model, the thrusters, to our advantage. The key benefit of our approach is that unlike other optimization-based nonlinear control methods, performance-related constraints are met during the single-support phase without reliance on costly numerical methods. Furthermore, the proposed thruster-assisted gait control framework allows for the utilization of performance and robustness-enhancing capabilities during particular phases of the gait cycle, a previously unreported aspect. Ultimately, our approach has been designed to be broadly applicable to a variety of bipedal robots across different scenarios. To validate our approach, simulated thruster-assisted gait testing was conducted using the ATLAS robot, the results of which are presented in this paper. The findings demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in ensuring the robust hybrid invariance of supported phases of bipedal robots assisted by thrusters. The associated controller and filter code has been made available within the paper's supplementary materials. The code is built using MATLAB/Simulink, with additional utility scripts created using Python 2.7, with the underlying ATLAS robot simulations based on realistic biomechanical models constructed using Visual3D, a professional 3D full-body gait analysis capture and simulation system. The primary research presented within this paper has been conceived and initially explored as part of a broader project aimed at developing efficient optimized control systems for bipedal robots assisted by thrusters, a topic that requires further research across various key aspects before the associated techniques can be considered mature. The current approach has been created with the intention of providing a usable solution for existing robotic platforms rather than serving as a foundation for further refinement. Notwithstanding these limitations, the present version remains viable for application to a range of existing bipedal robots across different scenarios, as evidenced by the results obtained from simulated testing using the ATLAS robot. This discovery motivated further research into the properties of a specific mathematical theory related to valued fields. In the course of these investigations, the authors proved that this theory does not have a certain desirable feature and demonstrated that, for infinite fields $k$, the associated power series fields cannot be computationally decided. This, in turn, led to an analogous undecidability conclusion for a specific complex-valued field of power series. In addition, the authors established that the ring of integers from the field of $p$-adic numbers cannot be computationally determined for any prime number $p$. This specific undecidability result was initially discovered by Rauzy in a more limited context. Moreover, the authors extended and refined the Becker-Denef-Lipschitz findings to include fields of positive characteristic and demonstrated that the associated power series fields cannot be computationally decided.
