In order to enhance side-channel attacks, this research introduces a new technique, HyperDegrade, which incorporates previous methods and employs simultaneous multithreading architectures.  A novel analysis into the causes of performance degradation through cache eviction was also performed, leading to the discovery of an unknown source of slowdowns.  Compared to existing techniques, HyperDegrade resulted in more significant slowdowns and improvements, which in certain cases achieved an enhanced time granularity of three orders of magnitude for Flush+Reload attacks.  To further evaluate the technique, metrics for side-channel leakage were proposed, which demonstrated that HyperDegrade could be effective in side-channel amplification without compromising data integrity.  A fair comparison between three different performance degradation strategies in combination with Flush+Reload attacks revealed HyperDegrade's efficacy, which enabled the development of an attack on an OpenSSL vulnerability three times more efficient than other methods.  In addition, HyperDegrade's applicability to Raccoon-like attacks was also demonstrated, which can succeed with real-world data and extend the scope of existing attacks to various protocols, filling in the gap left by previous research.  A possible limitation of the technique was discovered, which could limit HyperDegrade's applicability to recent processor models, yet it remains viable for widely used older models.  In conclusion, this research has made multiple contributions to the field of side-channel attacks, including an innovative technique, valuable insights, a performance evaluation, and an attack scenario that can be replicated with real-world data.  The results obtained are encouraging, suggesting the value of further exploring the intersection of side-channel attacks and performance degradation techniques in the context of low-level memory management.  The project's source code has been made available openly for the benefit of the computing community.  Future work is proposed, such as the extension of HyperDegrade to recent processor models and the investigation of its applicability to other attacks and systems, with the aim of providing a solid foundation for side-channel attack amplification through performance degradation in full generality.  A detailed guide for replicating the project's results has been included in the appendix section.  The project's results have been presented at the EuroS&P conference in 2022 following a rigorous review process.  The research underlying this project was funded by the National Science Foundation in the United States under grant number 2038947.  Any opinions expressed herein are solely those of the authors.  This research was also supported by the Cyber Security Research Center at Ben-Gurion University in Israel.

We've demonstrated that combining the 1-cocycle of a long knot's space with Fox-Hatcher 1-cycles through integration produces a specific Vassiliev invariant, having a precise order of three. This discovery builds on a preceding finding by the second listed author, proving that I(X) integrated over the Gramain 1-cycles generates the Casson invariant, a singular, nontrivial Vassiliev invariant of order two after accounting for scalar multiplication factors. Similarities can be drawn with a part of Mortier's research. Nonetheless, in contrast to but also inspired by his result, we derive our cocycle, I(X), through the use of graph-based configuration space integrals rather than combinatorial approaches used by Mortier. Additionally, we reveal that the cocycle I(X) when applied to links yields invariants that correspond to aspects of a specific, more complex Vassiliev invariants known as the "second self-linking invariant of a knot", also known as the "Kauffman bracket skein relation invariant". It's worth noting that these particular invariants are distinct from but closely related to the ones defined through classical Reidemeister moves in the field of knot theory. We also propose a possible method to determine the cocycle I(X) directly from the definition of a long knot's space, which could be valuable for extending and modifying the current approach. A notable connection can be observed between the introduced invariants and the one generated by combining the volume of the knot's space with the Janssens-Zagier differential operator, particularly when considering links. However, the resulting differential operator's image does not generate cocycles similar to I(X), which are distinct from but related to the ones produced by the volume of the knot's space. Consequently, this discovery highlights the uniqueness of the introduced invariants. A brief discussion on the relationship between these discovered invariants and other mathematical concepts such as the composite volume, the second differential operator, and the volume's gradient, is also provided. Lastly, possible future extensions and generalizations of the current approach are proposed. Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring an unnecessarily large number of features, directly proportional to the size of the dataset, in order to achieve satisfactory results comparable to traditional kernel-based methods. In order to circumvent these limitations and efficiently process large datasets, this paper introduces an alternative method of kernel approximation that leverages insights specific to the underlying data and offers both feature dimensionality reduction and performance enhancements. We test and evaluate this novel method against a range of competitors, including RFF, orthogonal random features, and the Nyström method. Interestingly, our method is found to consistently outperform RFF, often to a significant degree, and also exhibits comparable performance to the Nyström method, thus demonstrating its potential as a highly effective and efficient kernel approximation technique, particularly in scenarios involving large datasets. In addition to its applications in machine learning, this method also has implications for other areas of research, such as signal processing and numerical linear algebra. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Moreover, our approach achieves realistic results on real-world faces with extensive occlusions. Our code is available at https://github.com/zwang84/SADRNet.

In recent years, significant progress made by large-scale models has underscored the relevance of statistical models featuring multiple parameters. Research has been conducted to evaluate linear models with numerous parameters in high-dimensional environments characterized by non-sparse data. These studies typically assume the independence of data samples, but the current research extends beyond this limitation by exploring a linear regression model with time series data under conditions of over-parameterization, where data samples are inherently interdependent. The study develops an interpolation-based estimator and associated risk theory that accommodates varying levels of data interdependence, infinite data dimensions lacking sparsity, and both short and long-memory processes. The theoretical risk analysis leverages the concept of integrated covariance along with non-degeneracy properties of autocorrelation matrices. The results demonstrate comparable risk convergence rates to those in independent settings for short-memory processes and significantly slower convergence rates for long-memory processes. The research also illustrates specific, applicable examples of dependent processes. The proposed estimator and associated theory can be applied to a broader range of linear models featuring time-varying coefficients, multiple latent factors, and nonlinear transformations. The current research builds upon previous findings regarding the convergence rates of risks in linear regression models with dependent processes, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the interplay between data interdependence, convergence rates, and model complexity. The study offers an original contribution to the existing literature by extending the conventional independent data framework. The research has implications for various applications, such as the analysis of financial time series data, molecular profiles, and web text data. The associated code and results are available on the repository at https://github.com/YiluoZhong/linear_model_dependent_data. A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. Given the inherent difficulty of modifying a storage unit's risk preferences, our recommendation is to consider alternative risk-management strategies, such as pricing protocols that account for risk or market participation incentives, in order to encourage healthy participation of storage units in the electricity market. In addition, our results provide valuable insights into developing more accurate expectations of storage units' behavior. Our empirical analysis also reveals that storage units frequently fail to fulfill their scheduled energy allocations, yet the penalty fees associated with non-compliance are generally too low to act as a deterrent. This has important policy implications for designing suitable pricing schemes that balance the trade-offs between encouraging healthy participation, managing risk, and preventing non-compliance. Our recommendations can be applied to existing and emerging markets with storage units in the electricity sector. Our empirical evidence and analytical approach can also be applied to other markets featuring storage units with similar risk-averse characteristics. Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized resistance emerged at low magnetic field strength due to Landau filling, and was closely related to helical edge states that form around the neutral point of the samples. Conversely, larger samples showed significant resistance oscillations in low-magnetic-field conditions. This behavior is attributed to interaction between the neutral state at the edge and a non-neutral hole Landau level within the bulk material. A hypothetical model incorporating a reservoir formed by heavy holes has been developed as an explanatory framework. All measurements were conducted at low temperature (1.5 K) using a lock-in technique with a 10 $\mu$A excitation current. A specially designed, flux-compensated, six-probe resistor was used to minimize the influence of any residual magnetic field on results. Moreover, our approach can be easily expanded to account for various TDD scheduling modes and various types of cellular infrastructure. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the benefits of dynamic TDD scheduling, despite its difficulties, and offers a viable solution for future cellular networks with increasing traffic demands and varying local conditions. Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. Furthermore, our proposed method demonstrates comparable performance to other robust learning techniques while requiring significantly less data, as shown in comparative experiments using real-world datasets. We have made the code and models available for public use. Word embeddings, which convert textual information into numerical data, are a fundamental tool in natural language processing, enabling machines to understand and process text. However, the current most advanced word embedding techniques require substantial amounts of text data to function effectively, posing a challenge for applications involving limited amounts of data, such as personalized text classification, where collecting extensive amounts of personal data is impractical. In response to this limitation, a novel automatic word embedding generator has been developed, capable of producing high-quality word embeddings for any sentence based solely on its linguistic structure and patterns of similar sentences, without the need for additional training. This approach leverages a generative pre-trained transformer model, incorporating additional features such as part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, and sentence similarity information, to enhance the accuracy of word embeddings by capturing both local grammatical characteristics and global semantic similarities. As a result, it outperforms existing methods in tasks like sentiment analysis, text classification, and language modeling, according to comprehensive comparative experiments conducted using various datasets. Moreover, the proposed generator exhibits robust performance when operating in low-data scenarios, as it can effectively utilize general knowledge to inform its predictions, as demonstrated by successful deployments in both synthetic and real-world settings. A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. In the process, we establish a relationship between $J_n^T$ and the original colored Jones polynomial, thereby confirming volume conjecture behavior also applies to the latter. In contrast to the latter, $J_n^T$ is revealed to be a non-trivial, distinct polynomial for trivial links, offering an implication for its volume conjecture behavior. In addition, $J_n^T$ can be interpreted as an invariant for closed, semi-simple, locally compact topological groups via a construction rooted in quantum geometry. In this context, it is linked to the original colored Jones polynomial through the relationship between Chern-Simons and Kirchhoff modules. In the process, we establish an instance of volume conjecture behavior related to the eigenvalue of the Casimir operator in the representation of the fundamental group. Furthermore, $J_n^T$ yields an instance of non-trivial volume conjecture behavior associated with Bannai-Ito pairs, providing a connection to its construction as a polynomial for virtual links. In this context, it is demonstrated that the relation between the eigenvalue of the Bannai-Ito operator and the volume conjecture can be generalized to a broader context of quantum invariants linked to algebraic geometry, specifically to the properties of Hecke operators on curves. In this setting, the relation is shown to be a result of the composition of the curvature of the connection associated with the Fock-Goncharov construction, combined with the action of the monodromy of the local system generated by the Hecke operators. In this process, it is revealed that the volume conjecture can be extended to a broader context of quantum invariants linked to algebraic geometry, specifically to the properties of Hecke operators on curves.

The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. Additionally, measurements were obtained for single top quark production in the same final-state configuration, at an estimated 5 nanobarns with a 3-nanobarns precision, also aligning with predicted values from quantum chromodynamics. These results demonstrate the capability of the CMS experiment to study heavy quark production in heavy-ion collisions and provide a foundation for further research. The investigation of top quark decay into bottom quark plus a light quark or lepton pair was also conducted as well as searches for rare top quark decay processes such as the decay into a photon or a gluon plus a light quark or lepton pair, however these research endeavors are considered preliminary due to relatively low event counts involved. The corresponding cross-sectional measurements for these rare top quark production processes were found to be 1 picobarn, 0.46 picobarn, 0.33 picobarn, and 0.29 picobarn with respect to the inelastic lead-nucleon center-of-mass energy, however these results are also considered preliminary due to limited amounts of collected data. The research on heavy quark production also led to the establishment of a lower limit on the lifetime of the top quark of 0.75 nanoseconds, surpassing the previously established limit of 0.33 nanoseconds, and the measurement of the W-boson top quark decay ratio as 0.421 or 68% confident in the range 0.356 to 0.486. The annealed large deviation principle (LDP) for the empirical process of words is characterized by a rate function that equals the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of words with respect to the reference distribution of words.  For renewal times with an algebraic tail, a quenched LDP (conditioned on a typical sequence of letters) was established by Birkner, Greven, and den Hollander, which resulted in a rate function consisting of two components, including the annealed rate function and another component proportional to the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of letters relative to the reference distribution of letters, obtained by combining the words and randomizing the starting point.  The proportionality constant was found to be equal to the tail exponent of the renewal process.  The purpose of this study is to extend both LDPs to sequences of letters that are not independent and identically distributed by demonstrating that both principles can be applied to sequences of letters satisfying a condition known as summable variation, which provides the necessary condition for both principles to be applicable, while neither of the reference laws involved in the rate functions is independent and identically distributed.  The result also holds for a single sequence of words that is not independent and identically distributed. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. Experimental findings confirm our proposed approach yields superior results than conventional methods, as measured by the accuracy achieved and the computational time required. We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which we found significantly enhances Bucket Elimination by substantially reducing the computational time and memory usage. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, as well as CPLEX, GUROBI and toulbar2 for constrained optimisation, by achieving a 5 orders of magnitude improvement in our experiments following a widely established evaluation procedure. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol found that for these two systems, viscosity can be condensed into a singular, stress- and volume fraction-independent curve, revealing distinct scaling regimes that reflect different universality classes and implying that isotropic and anisotropic shear jamming have unique characteristics. Furthermore, by integrating the effects of microscale interactions into a dimensionless variable that gauges the distance from shear jamming, scientists have paved the way for applying theories developed for equilibrium phenomena to better understand the physics governing the shear thickening transition. Ultimately, this work lays the groundwork for a unified understanding of the complex interactions governing fluid-like and rigid-like states of matter, with implications for applying simplified models to realistic systems of real interest. Nonetheless, certain limitations of this study, such as the lack of inclusion of time as an key factor, also need to be addressed in the future. Ultimately, this study suggests that even dense mixtures exhibiting non-Newtonian behavior can be classified using the same principles that govern Newtonian fluids, challenging the conventional notion that these systems require distinct physical descriptions. An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work on the Web. This study examines public sector officials' reliance on Google's Web search engine for their assessment, their knowledge of potential biases in search algorithms and the influence they have on retrieving all relevant information. The study's results show that a substantial number of the participants are unaware of potential biases in search algorithms and the possible strategies to prevent them from overlooking essential information. Notably, our data reveal that as much as 20% of the necessary information may go undetected due to the influence of Web search personalisation. This study's findings highlight the significance of Web search for public sector professionals, suggesting the necessity for training on search algorithms' potential biases that can shape judgments and decisions. In addition, it is crucial that these professionals are provided with guidelines to reduce the likelihood of missing relevant information. This study's implications for its public sector context are also discussed, along with its broader implications for other professional settings that heavily rely on Web search. In these settings, search personalisation can significantly influence assessments, judgments and decision-making, prompting the need for ongoing education and policy guidelines that mitigate its harmful effects. In short, this study demonstrates the substantial impact that Web search personalisation can have on professional work, suggesting the necessity for a critical examination of search algorithms and potential strategies to reduce the likelihood of missing essential information. This examination can be intricate, yet it is indispensable in search of solutions that minimize the harmful consequences of search personalisation on professional work, informed by a thorough understanding of its underlying mechanisms, the ethical principles that guide professional work and the specific contexts in which it takes place. This study's results and discussions are based on in-depth interviews with 20 public sector officials in Ireland, who were selected through a multi-stage process that began with a nationwide recruitment drive. The study's participants span different professions, ages, genders and levels of experience, thereby enhancing the validity of its findings. This research is part of the larger WISDOM project, a comprehensive research project that aims to improve the effectiveness of Web search for public sector professionals through better search interfaces and reduced search personalisation, by examining the underlying mechanisms that influence assessments, judgments and decision-making, informed by a critical examination of ethical principles that guide professional work. This study's findings can be utilized by policymakers, search engine companies and researchers working towards the development of search engines that are more transparent, fair and effective for professional work, by reducing the harmful consequences of search personalisation.

A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. Parameters for low-resolution reconstruction, including resolution and regularization, were optimally selected through a grid search method. The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. Moreover, we've made the underlying source code of our algorithm publicly available for others to use. Finally, we've conducted a rigorous evaluation of our algorithm to demonstrate its accuracy, stability, and speedup advantages over existing approximation methods. We recommend using the exact paired-permutation test algorithm in place of Monte Carlo approximations in future NLP systems. A comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping quantities, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship prices has been assembled from 1966 to 2009 for the six primary shipping routes. Furthermore, instructions on combining and verifying datasets are provided using the knowledge of shipping industry specialists and former top executives. A descriptive analysis of previously unstudied market phenomena known as the "container crisis" is conducted with this data. Structural changes in the data variables are then identified to demonstrate how the dissolution of shipping monopolies affected market behavior. Key findings reveal that removing entry barriers increased efficiency, yet it also created risks of market failures that can lead to significant costs for industry participants. A theoretical model highlighting the importance of distinguishing between new and used ship prices is also discussed. Lastly, an empirical examination of shipping industry market power is conducted with results indicating that strong market power existed until the arrival of massive new ship supplies in 1998, and even then, residual market power persisted until 2004. A bonus analysis of scrubbed ship prices adds value to this study by illustrating how shipping industry executives successfully colluded to manipulate prices by destroying existing ships, and the costs saved from such actions were evenly split between shipowners and operators. Notably, this deception was possible due to inadequate anti-trust enforcement in the shipping industry at the time. No significant market power was found in the six primary shipping routes after 2004, yet the residual power that persisted during this period took the form of higher prices for smaller ship sizes and higher fees for demolition services. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the validity of applying modern shipping industry data to economic theories and models, and it paves the way for ongoing research into important economic questions surrounding market power, efficiency, and performance. The methodology used can be applied to other capital goods markets with similar characteristics. The combined dataset is currently the most comprehensive of its kind, spanning over four decades with daily observations for key shipping industry variables, and it is accompanied by detailed documentation necessary for replication in various contexts. The data and program files necessary for the analysis conducted in this research are available for public use with the hope of informing ongoing debates in economics education and research. The combined dataset has been made available to the public domain by the seller with the aim of informing ongoing debates in economics education and research. We define loom spaces as a more general framework incorporating leaf spaces for pseudo-Anosov flows and link spaces for veering triangulations. Building on Gu\'eritaud's research, it is demonstrated that there is a veering triangulation inherently linked to every loom space, with this triangulation's realization being topologically equivalent to 3D space. Additionally, it is shown that each loom space can be characterized by a specific kind of veering triangulation, with this characterization being inherently distinct from its counterpart defined by Thurston's full circle theorem. Furthermore, a method for calculating volume is introduced within this context. Moreover, it is proven that the volume of a loom space is identical to the sum of the volumes of its constituent veering triangulations. Lastly, it is demonstrated that the sharp ratio of a loom space, defined as the ratio of its volume to the minimum possible volume, can be calculated and is specifically shown to be 1 for certain types of loom spaces known as fill looms. Consequently, it is also proven that the minimum possible volume of any loom space is equivalent to the sum of the volumes of its constituent veering triangulations. A significant implication arising from this finding is that the minimum possible volume of any veering triangulation is solely dependent on the underlying surface it is constructed upon, thereby establishing a distinct volume category for veering triangulations that is distinct from those with volume ratio greater than 1. It is also noteworthy that the volume of a loom space can be determined by calculating the volume of its corresponding pseudo-Anosov flow, as well as by calculating the sum of the volumes of its constituent veering triangulations. By contrast, the volume of a veering triangulation cannot be determined from the volume of the underlying surface it is constructed upon. It is also observed that there is a significant volume disparity exhibited by veering triangulations, particularly those constructed from fill looms, with one example displaying a volume ratio of 2, thereby illustrating the distinct volume category mentioned earlier. It is also worth noting that research on the volume of veering triangulations was previously conducted by Puerzer-Hauertl, Gueritaud, and Bonner, although the scope of their studies was limited to volumes of veering triangulations constructed from fill looms. This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs physics. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our primary analysis concerns the double Higgs production process in the two EFTs through the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess for all polarization channels and relevant effective operators at various energies, and demonstrate how in the HEFT case, the cross-section primarily depends on two leading coefficients at these TeV scales. We then establish the equivalence between the dominant coefficients of the HEFT and SMEFT at the level of the scattering amplitude for this subprocess. In the subsequent analysis, we explore the detectability of the two leading HEFT coefficients at the two planned colliders CLIC (operating at 3 TeV, 5 ab$^{-1}$) and ILC (operating at 1 TeV, 8 ab$^{-1}$), and identify the accessible parameter regions by studying the predicted rates for the characteristic four bottom jet signatures with missing energy in the $b \bar b b \bar b \nu \bar \nu$ final state. Ultimately, we find that at the 1 TeV ILC, the most sensitive region lies in the plane defined by large enhancements of the effective operators $S$ and $T$, while at the 3 TeV CLIC, the most prominent signals can be found in the planes characterized by the effective operators $W$, $W^\dagger$ and $S$, $T$ simultaneously. We emphasize that at both planned colliders, the relevant effective operators can be probed with an accuracy of better than 10\%. We also highlight the future potential of these colliders to distinguish between the two EFTs by considering additional Higgs boson decay modes in the $b \bar b \gamma \gamma$ and $b \bar b \tau^+ \tau^-$ final states. Ultimately, we contend that the investigation of double Higgs production within the framework of EFTs is crucial for uncovering beyond-Standard Model Higgs physics at future colliders. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Moreover, the researchers develop a new time-stepping scheme that is both conservative and dissipative at the same time, and showcase the practical utility of the method by applying it to the conservation of energy in the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. Furthermore, various test cases are presented to illustrate the effectiveness of this new approach. This study further delves into the relationship between the iteration tolerance and the error associated with property preservation, and investigates the impact of different time-stepping schemes on this associated error. Finally, the researchers explore different iteration methods including the quasi-Newton method, the transverse method, and the iterative Newton method, among others. This study also examines the connection between the convergence of the iteration method and the associated error, and presents numerical results for different systems of equations. This approach is further applicable to a broad range of applications involving time-dependent PDEs. This research paves the way for developing efficient preconditioning techniques that can significantly reduce the number of iteration required to achieve a desirable level of precision. This study also highlights the potential applications of this new approach to other numerical methods such as exponential time-stepping methods, implicit-explicit time-stepping methods, and fluid-structure interactions, among others. Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs during testing. The trained network provides an optimal displacement field to map preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface, demonstrated by multiple experiments showing its applicability and efficiency with real-world data. The developed code is now openly accessible online.

Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. We introduce a unique method, Adversarial Metric Learning, for self-supervised flow estimation where two models work in tandem: one performs flow estimation and another derives a latent metric to differentiate the altered points from the target point cloud, achieved through a Multi-Scale Triplet loss calculation using intermediate feature vectors. We leverage our benchmark to gain insight into various models and our proposed framework, finding that our method successfully preserves spatial coherence and detailed geometric structures, whereas many self-supervised baselines fail in this aspect. Nonetheless, overcoming occlusions remains a significant challenge. We anticipate that our dataset and the proposed method will serve as a foundation for future research on self-supervised flow estimation. Our code and dataset are available at: \url{https://github.com/Yuehubin/Self-Flow}.

A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure. Finally, we demonstrate that the PMH-property is not a necessary condition for the E2F property by presenting an example of a non-bipartite cubic graph that satisfies the E2F condition but not the PMH-property. Our extensive research also reveals that the term even-2-factorability (E2F) is interchangeable with the term 2-acyclic, which refers to graphs whose all 2-factors are cyclic. Our work on the papillon graph family provides an infinite generation of both 2-acyclic and E2F cubic graphs, expanding the previously limited collection of such graphs that include the Gras cube and the Heawood cube. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a more limited system call filter, is comparable to that of an unsecured system. Ultimately, Timeloops system call learning can be an important resource for future secure containerized applications following microservice architecture. The source code for Timeloops is available at https://timeloops.cs.berkeley.edu/.

High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations of the wave equation solver are feasible. Despite these developments, the challenge of the large storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations remains, and two possible workaround strategies for reducing this demand are proposed, including extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data rather than wavefields. Ultimately, the feasibility of both WRI and ESI is tested on synthetic data sets of realistic seismic reflection data quantities and configurations, and the results indicate that both methods are capable of reconstructing accurate subsurface models despite starting from incorrectly simulated data, and the challenge of the large storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations remains.  Additionally, the impact of various inversion parameters on the performance of both methods is also examined in detail. The final outcome confirms the promising potential of both WRI and ESI techniques as viable alternatives to traditional FWI methods. The code used in this research is available at https://github.com/ying789798/wri_esi. The model's results are discussed in the context of current species competition theories and the need for further research on the impact of different dispersal patterns among species. This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network, which incorporates D2D communication. This hybrid network allows a central hub to transfer data to those in need and supply power to those who require it. This coexistence also allows D2D transmissions to use the same bandwidth. This integrated network is critical in addressing future energy and spectrum shortages. However, these D2D transmissions and wireless link losses could significantly impede the data transfer rate. In response to this challenge, we propose introducing an intelligent reflecting surface. We then develop an optimization problem to maximize the data transfer rate while ensuring that power is generated and D2D communication speeds are met. This optimization problem requires significant computational resources, but we develop an algorithm that addresses this challenge with reduced computational demands. Finally, simulations confirm the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm. These simulations demonstrate how the proposed algorithm compares to other existing solutions and provide valuable insights into key parameters that influence this integrated network. This research has far-reaching implications for the development of future energy- and spectrum-scarce networks. It also highlights the potential of integrated data and energy transmission networks in addressing future challenges. This research paves the way for further exploration into various aspects of this integrated network, including its security and potential applications. The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate

alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 1 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design features 
(fill-factor, pixel pattern, symmetry), we identify how they influence the electron 
probe size and current density. Our proposed designs exhibit probe sizes ($d_{50}$) 
as low as 0.66 Angstrom, indicating that a programmable phase plate with 
electrostatic elements can successfully rectify spherical aberration well beyond the 
1 Angstrom threshold. Furthermore, our designs offer large enough central beam 
intensities to support optimal imaging conditions. Given the simplicity and 
flexibility of our designs, we suggest exploring various modifications, such as 
using multi-layer elements, to potentially enhance the phase plate's performance.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes a Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state. Based on this spectrum, we establish criteria for the spectral stability of solitary waves. Specifically, we show that if the anharmonic oscillator's on-site interaction is either sufficiently negative or positive, the solitary wave state is spectrally stable. Conversely, if this interaction lies within the $(-4,0]$ interval, the solitary wave state is spectrally unstable. Notably, in the unstable interval, the linearized equation's spectrum contains a continuous band of positive eigenvalues, and we conjecture that this instance of spectral instability implies orbital instability in accordance with a significant orbital stability criterion. Nonetheless, we encounter an instance of orbital instability that is not explained by the anharmonic oscillator's anharmonicity, demonstrating that an analog of the Shukhovitch condition is essential for ensuring the orbital stability of solutions to a combined anharmonic oscillator-Klein-Gordon system. We also investigate the anharmonic oscillator's anharmonicity's impact on the combined system's orbital stability, finding that this anharmonicity causes the anharmonic oscillator to emit energy at the same rate as it scatters solitary waves, thereby precluding the orbital instability observed in its isolated form. We also observe that the anharmonic oscillator's anharmonicity accelerates the anharmonic oscillator's solutions towards equilibrium in accordance with a harmonic oscillator-like law, allowing us to apply a specific harmonic oscillator stability theory to determine the anharmonic oscillator's solution's stability. Finally, we apply our general spectral stability criteria to the combined system to conclude that if the anharmonic oscillator's on-site interaction lies within the $(-4,0]$ interval, the combined system's solution suffers from an anomaly: the anomaly of continuous spectrum-induced instability, which is revealed through numerical means and is characterized by an unusual destruction mechanism of the solitary wave solution due to the generation of a continuous positive eigenvalue spectrum in the linearized equation at the solitary wave state. We also discover that this anomaly leads to the combined system suffering from an anomaly of continuous spectrum-induced orbital instability in addition to the lack of an analog of the Shukhovitch condition, making it an example of a Hamiltonian system that is not protected against the destruction caused by the generation of positive eigenvalues in the linearized equation at the solitary wave

We derive new conclusions regarding the additive Galois module properties of specific wildly ramified finite non-abelian extensions of Q. Notably, in cases where K/Q is a Galois extension with a Galois group isomorphic to A4, S4 or A5, we determine essential and sufficient criteria for the ring of integers in K to be freely generated over its associated order within the rational group algebra constructed from the Galois group G. Our evidence suggests that these criteria are also indicative of additive Galois module properties for related modular forms and Eisenstein series. Our study also involves an exhaustive examination of prior results on this subject, as well as the introduction of a novel approach that combines the theory of relative trace functions and the use of plane curves with simple singularities to address these problems. Furthermore, our findings are illustrated through explicit computations of certain ring structures associated with well-defined pairs of fields, including examples drawn from the family of extensions generated by the Coxeter-Norton family, as well as certain notable members of this family, including the degrees known as $S_4^{1a}$ and $A_5^{2b}$. Additionally, we demonstrate how our findings can be connected to results obtained using other approaches, as well as how they impact our understanding of particular configurations of parameters that define the Coxeter-Norton family of extensions. Our research has originated several interesting questions that are relevant to future investigations, including questions related to the frame of reference, new consequences for number theory, as well as connections to the geometry of plane curves and the modularity of certain automorphic forms. Our findings have been published in multiple papers, including an earlier paper titled "The Ring of Integers of Galois Extensions with Specific Finite Non-Abelian Groups", as well as two separate papers titled "Additive Galois Module Properties of S_4 and A_5 Extensions" and "Approaches to Solving Polynomials with Coefficients in the Rational Group Algebra Q[G]". Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear model that links radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the conversion of values, relativistic beaming effects, and the characteristics of the AGN system, we determine the minimum possible spins of heavy jetted AGNs. These results help explore the relationship between the masses of ultra-light scalar, vector, and tensor particles, closing a gap in parameter space around $10^{-20}-10^{-19}$eV. Additionally, we determine the upper limits on the decay constant of axions, assuming their decay could prevent their entry into a state of instability and their possible non-observation through superradiance. This research also provides upper limits on the fraction of dark matter comprised by ultra-light axion-like particles, concluding that, as a single species, such a particle cannot constitute more than 10% of the dark matter in a given mass range ($10^{-21} < \mu \, (\mathrm{eV}) < 10^{-17}$). This occurs when considering a wide range of potentials, including the non-relativistic elastic scattering of neutrinos off nucleons and their conversion from dark radiation. This research underlines the significance of studying the properties of ultra-light particles, particularly those that could be found within the reach of upcoming experiments, such as the next-generation double beta decay experiments and axion helioscopes. A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging
techniques in live zebrafish retinas during initial development to gain insights into the underlying mechanisms governing
the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to accurately map the migration
patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop and test
a hypothesis that retinal IKNM is driven by a diffusive process fueled by the accumulation of new nuclei at the upper
retinal surface. Our results demonstrate how the tight packing of nuclei at the upper surface influences their movement
patterns, provide a reliable, quantifiable explanation for the uneven distribution of nuclei across the retina, and may
have implications for random cell fate selection within this system. Furthermore, we find evidence suggesting that the
retinal IKNM's radial gradient is crucial for maintaining the proper, curved shape of the neuroepithelial tissue. Our study
offers a comprehensive exploration of the interkinetic nuclear migration mechanism in the developing zebrafish retina.

In various image processing tasks, including video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, images must be separated from coded measurements that represent their superposition. Real-world code patterns, which are often non-negative, systematically structured and non-Gaussian, can impede reconstruction performance due to their non-ideal coherence properties. Contrary to previous assumptions, the dynamics of this specific class of active matter cannot be accurately captured using simplified hydrodynamic models when the spatial environment is two-dimensional up to five-dimensional space; however, we were able to derive precise, dimension-dependent scaling parameters for these dimensions. Furthermore, our research reveals the presence of a critical threshold for the average spacing between inclusions, beyond which the collective velocity decreases significantly, in accordance with a power law that is dependent on the dimensional context. In addition, our theoretical framework predicts the existence of a unique, non-zero scalar amplitude in the correlation function of the local active tendency in the most general sense, and this amplitude maintains an invariant value that is unaffected by changes in the dimensional context. In the absence of inclusions, our model mirrors previous hydrodynamic theory predictions for incompressible polar active fluids, and it includes the specific case where the spatial dimensions approach infinity. The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it necessary to convert printed documents into digital formats.  There has been an increase in fraudulent activities lately.  To prevent such account-related fraud, a system was devised which employs ID card extraction via OCR and NLP for verification purposes.  Optical Character Recognition, a technology that enables the conversion of images to text, can also be used to convert an Indonesian ID card or KTP into text format.  This facilitates easier data entry for service operators.  To enhance accuracy, the extracted text was further corrected using Natural Language Processing.  When tested using 50 Indonesian ID card images, the F-score achieved was 0.78, and the extraction process for each ID card took approximately 4510 milliseconds.  This ID card extraction technology can be utilized as part of a verification process that also involves citizen biometrics such as fingerprint or face recognition.  To demonstrate its applicability, a system prototype was devised which enables citizens to upload their ID cards, extract the text, and match it with their existing account information.  Should the information on the ID card be different from what is currently recorded, the system will prompt the customer to update the account information.  This way, even though the service is fully automated, it is still accurate and reliable.  This technology can be applied to any service that requires the verification of customer identity based on their ID card.  To operate the system, no special knowledge is required except for how to capture an ID card image using a mobile application.  This system was devised as part of a project to provide fully automated services at the Indonesian Immigration Office.  To evaluate its effectiveness, a user satisfaction survey was conducted among 120 citizens, with the results showing that 57% of them preferred this new service over traditional ones, and it reduced waiting time from one hour to just 15 minutes.  This approach can be applied to any public service that relies on ID card verification. Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations. The algorithm's efficiency was examined by comparing it to continuous-time simulations, both of which yielded comparable results. The efficiency of the lattice algorithm was found to increase significantly with growing lambda. It was also found that the algorithm efficiently samples the classical ring action, which minimizes the effective potential and accurately determines the real eigenvalues, but may experience difficulties with complex eigenvalues. The algorithm's performance improved with smaller time step parameters in simulations. The ring algorithm's efficiency proved insensitive to changes in the mass parameter. The sampling of the target state was found to be reliable, with the algorithm efficiently navigating the landscape of the effective potential, especially when the effective mass is high. The algorithm's performance degradation with increasing effective mass was examined, along with the importance of properly normalizing the target state to avoid bias towards lower energy eigenstates. The algorithm's performance in the driving force scenario was compared to an alternative approach using a semi-classical approximation, which deviated from the expected behavior in certain force intensities. The ring algorithm was found to be more reliable, with the added benefit of being a pure algorithm that doesn't require the user to adjust parameters to achieve accurate results. The algorithm's performance in the time-dependent driving force simulation demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing force intensities, along with the expected behavior in the expectation value of the position operator and the corresponding period of oscillation. The algorithm successfully sampled the target state even when the effective mass changed over time, with the associated loss of efficiency temporarily until the algorithm readjustes to the new effective mass. The algorithm's performance in this scenario was found to be robust, with the associated period of oscillation accurately determined. The performance of the algorithm was examined in more detail by comparing it to the continuous-time case, along with the results of theoretical predictions for the associated period of oscillation. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. By modeling the YORP effect and incorporating other relevant parameters into their analysis, scientists were able to detect the YORP acceleration in three asteroids and found that the YORP acceleration in all ten detected cases was positive, accelerating their rotations. Furthermore, incorporating solar precession into their algorithm revealed evidence of this phenomenon in the data obtained for Geographos, which may be a crucial feature that needs further explanation. The investigation into the thermal radiation patterns and the YORP effect acceleration of these asteroids is ongoing, as it is essential to improving the accuracy of predictions for their future rotational evolution. Additionally, this study has implications for identifying targets in a planned survey for the YORP effect in thousands of small asteroids by the Lucy mission, which will be launched in 2027 to explore Jupiter's orbit and provide further insights into the YORP effect in asteroids of similar sizes. The detected YORP acceleration in these specific asteroids ranges from 0.025 to 0.35 degrees per year, which is essential for predicting their future rotational states as effectively as possible, given the limited time the Lucy mission will spend on each target asteroid. The models developed during this research are valuable resources for conducting further investigations into the YORP effect acceleration, shape evolution, and rotation evolution of small asteroids like those found in the Lucy mission's target range. The observed light curves, model parameters, and YORP acceleration calculations are available for the three studied asteroids at the Planetary Data System, as well as the relevant software at public repositories on GitHub. The methodology used here can be applied to future observations of small asteroids and provides a framework for incorporating additional observations and models of the YORP effect and thermal radiation patterns into their analysis. The research into the YORP effect acceleration of small asteroids will continue, as it is crucial for accurately predicting their future rotational evolution, which in turn is essential for selecting relevant targets

Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that preserve regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to demonstrate that continuity can be reliably determined for rational and regular functions. Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement. 

Additionally, a more nuanced concept related to continuous functions is explored and related to its computable counterpart. Finally, some limitations and potential extensions to the current approach are considered, including the potential applications for developing more effective algorithms to decide the computability of specific functions. 

Lastly, some notable regular and rational function examples that are not continuous are identified, along with the recognition that for a function to be computable, it is not sufficient for the function to be regular or rational, as demonstrated by a more substantial class of functions that are both regular and rational but neither of these properties guarantees the function is computable.

A machine learning technique known as reservoir computing generates a model that mimics complex systems and can be trained on significantly smaller amounts of data compared to alternative methods. The latest version of this approach simplifies training by minimizing the need to adjust numerous parameters. In a recent experiment involving a highly complex system with distinct time scales and multiple coexisting patterns of behavior, a reservoir computer of the new design demonstrated several advantages over its traditional counterpart. Specifically, it used a much smaller amount of data for training, a much shorter time to adjust its performance, a smaller number of parameters to adjust, and a much higher level of accuracy in predicting patterns of behavior, even when those patterns change rapidly. In addition to this performance, it was able to predict areas of stability accurately, further confirming the benefits of this new algorithm. In contrast to other complex systems with different time scales and multiple coexisting patterns of behavior, by modifying the computer's dynamics, it was possible to demonstrate that a single reservoir computer is capable of accurately predicting a wide range of phenomena, even those that cannot be captured by alternative machine learning methods. To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints and worst-case disturbances in variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulations, we've developed a second-order successive sweep algorithm for calculating the reachable state space. This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control. We've proven the convergence and accuracy of our algorithm and demonstrated its effectiveness with multiple numerical examples featuring nonlinear and linear systems. Furthermore, we've found that this algorithm can be modified to solve a variation of the problem where the controller is allowed to change over time, providing an alternative solution to existing methods for this problem. This new approach has implications for optimal control in complex systems with multiple dynamic components and partial differential equations, as well as for safety-critical systems in applications such as transportation and robotics. This work also paves the way for extending the reachable state space algorithm to consider additional factors, such as stochastic disturbances and system uncertainties, by incorporating their effects into the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation. This approach can be implemented with relatively low computational demands, making it suitable for high-definition simulation of large-scale systems and real-time optimal control in systems with dynamic components. This is critical for enabling the safe and efficient operation of complex systems with changing components, for instance, in systems with gradual replacement of parts during operation. The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data indicated distinct posterior regions associated with each. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing multiple governing principles such as social agency that shape our understanding of this phenomenon. The methods used here can be applied to investigate the animacy spectrum in other populations and individuals with brain damage, providing a valuable tool for the study of VTC. The stimulus set and computational models developed here are available for public use. The study described in this paper has been published in the journal Neuroimage, volume 243, 2021. The study proves the nonexistence of Landau-Siegel zeros or confirms quantum unique ergodicity for GL_2 Hecke-Maass newforms at a calculable pace, supported by the broader conclusion that Dirichlet L-function zeros exert a force pushing zeros from all other automorphic L-functions off the s=1 axis. This research leverages two key tools: initially, it utilizes the idea that for any given Dirichlet character, altering the speed of its associated random walk results in a difference in depths of relevant zeros, leading to a contradiction if zeros of a given depth exist for multiple characters, thereby establishing the uniqueness of zeros from a specific depth, namely those deeper than 1; secondly, it introduces an alternative, equivalent approach based on the action of the Galois group on minimal orbits of a certain type of polynomial, known as monic, primitive, irreducible polynomials with coefficients in the rational numbers, ultimately allowing for an examination of the relationship between the coefficients of such polynomials and the associated zero locations, facilitating the conclusion that there are no landau-siegel zeros. This work also explores additional properties of these zeros, discussing alternative descriptions involving the moments of characteristic polynomials of random matrix ensembles, as well as the related discussion on the topic of quantum unique ergodicity for Hecke-Maass newforms, and finally, it touches on the connection between these zeros and the distribution of the characteristic polynomial of random matrix ensembles, including Hecke-Liouville matrices and the Gaussian unitary ensemble Sine-process. The study along these lines can be found in a companion paper titled "The extremal structure of Dirichlet L-function zeros".
