This study may serve as a starting point for further development aimed at fully automating application processing processes. It also highlights potential future work, such as integrating additional tasks and processes involved in application processing, and presents potential future directions, such as utilizing machine learning to enhance panel creation based on candidate evaluations. This approach may lead to better plans, but would require additional data and a carefully designed evaluation framework. In these scenarios, evaluating candidates and matching them with available positions shares common challenges with recruitment. It also touches on potential applications in dynamic scenarios, such as team formation in gaming, collaborative projects, and emergency response teams. This involves integrating temporal factors and evaluating solutions based on future dynamics and changing criteria. This study's focus on interview planning is just a small aspect of a broader problem that encompasses candidate evaluation, matching, scheduling, assignment, and allocation tasks. Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computation, leading to a significant reduction of up to 50 times in computational costs compared to other methods. The accuracy of these analytic expressions is validated through a relevant mismatch metric and found to be sufficiently precise for the PTA parameter space of interest. Furthermore, we introduce an improved approach using spline interpolation to enhance the computation speed for specific narrow-band PTA datasets. The implementation of these findings in the GWecc package enables seamless access to searching for such eccentric signals within PTA datasets via the ENTERPRISE platform. The accuracy and efficiency of these methods are demonstrated through a study using simulated data from a simulated scenario modeled after the prospective sensitivity of the future PTA dataset anticipated from the Square Kilometre Array. The effective search techniques developed here can be generally applied to other TIA datasets involving narrow-band signals. The underlying eccen package itself can be used independently to interpret the results of TIA searches for eccentric signals. We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a second-class particle placed at the origin, will asymptotically converge to a velocity whose probability distribution is uniform across the interval $[-1,1]$ as time tends to infinity. This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process. The proof involves creating a marked process that represents the history of the second-class particle and demonstrating that it converges to a stationary Markov process, whose evolution and structure can be thoroughly examined. Notably, we find that the velocity of the second-class particle evolves through a birth-death process on the half-line, with zero being the unique stationary point, and its rate functions satisfy a wide range of fractional differentiability properties, including the subdiffusivity that leads to the uniform asymptotic velocity distribution. This achievement is made possible by using recent results on the extremal length of a family of curves to analyze the formation of the marked process. Furthermore, we discover that the velocity process has coordinating branches, which enables us to apply the Feller property and explore its fractional behavior. Ultimately, this characterization allows us to determine the uniform asymptotic velocity distribution by examining the ergodic structure of the stationary Markov process. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated by interpreting the resulting asymptotic velocity distribution as a result of a specific branching process rather than an explicit computation. This technique can be applied more broadly, as we observe that the asymptotic behavior of the velocity process represents a more general class of self-similar processes with stationary increments that converge to a linear process, whose probability distribution is uniform across any interval as time tends to infinity. This generalization also enables us to recast the result from "The TASEP speed process" in terms of the extremal length of a family of curves, which is shown to converge to a constant as time tends to infinity. This convergence can be alternatively expressed as the convergence of the velocity process to a specific branching process, which is more broadly representative of the dynamics observed in ASEP and similar systems. This more general interpretation is made possible by re-expressing the velocity process in terms of the branching process, whose coordinates correspond to the branches of the tree that contribute to the asymptotic velocity distribution. This interpretation is a result of re-expressing the velocity process as a result of a random walk on the tree, whose stationary distribution is the asymptotic velocity distribution. This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control. Despite the variety of models reviewed, common challenges and limitations of current approaches are discussed, along with future research directions, especially the need for open-source software for model analysis and parameter estimation in response to global health crises. As with all living things, humans are susceptible to diseases caused by viruses, bacteria, fungi, and other microorganisms that can affect a single part of the body (surface or superficial) or multiple systems (deep-seated). Although diseases are an inevitable part of life, affecting people of all ages, certain age groups are more vulnerable than others. This report focuses on age-related factors that influence disease susceptibility in children, adults, and older adults, considering the interactions between age, performance of the immune system, cellular changes, functional capabilities, and various physiological changes that occur over time. Furthermore, it examines the concepts of senescence, immunosenescence, and cellular aging to provide a comprehensive understanding of the biological processes that underlie increased susceptibility to diseases as people age. We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. In our study, we also investigate the impact of light-based association and initial magnetization when a precise condition is met. Furthermore, we explored two scenarios: one in which the dark state condition is met imperfectly, either generally known as the adiabatic case, or not at all. In the adiabatic case, we derived an inelastic non-rigid pendulum model, which enables discussion on magnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum" as well as the emergence of large amplitude oscillations in molecule-atom pair entanglements. Lastly, we investigated an unusual scenario in which an initial sufficient magnitude of magnetization occurs, either naturally or artificially, where as a result of three-body recombination, large amplitude oscillations in molecule-atom pair entanglements develop their own rhythmic patterns due to the interplay between two- and three-body interactions within the condensate. Our research predictions are relevant to experimental investigations involving Bose-Einstein condensates of one spin unit, including potassium atoms demonstrated by LeBlanc et al., and suggested feasible experiments on spinless rubidium and cesium atoms. Our theoretical framework is a natural extension of previous studies on dark state conditions with two spin units by Jager, Goelen, and Dunning, which lacked an in-depth analysis of the adiabatic case. Our model for the adiabatic case also shares some similarities with a non-rigid pendulum model proposed by Dickerson, Hennies, Forster, and Simons, but with distinct physical applications. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects. Our approach also enables the restoration of damaged data through hierarchical segmentation, as fragments of a particular segment may be recovered from adjacent segments with compatible primer pairs. Our results show that with 1 Gb of DNA data stored in a segment that requires 3 Mb of sequencing to fully recover, we can reduce the sequencing cost from 4000-fold to 12.5-fold over a period of 11 days following initial investment costs of 10000-fold and 3000-fold, respectively. Additionally, we've found that with appropriate segment management, resequencing of the same segment can result in an increase in readable base pairs per day by as much as 1000x following an initial period of rapid degradation. Our approach has the added benefit of enabling the generation of partially overlapping segments, which can be considered as a form of fragment generation that can be utilized for various purposes, including the reconstruction of larger data objects from multiple, partially overlapping stored objects. Our research demonstrates the capability to store and efficiently manage large amounts of data using DNA, with adequate maintenance enabling ongoing use over an extended period. Our novel method has the potential to support infinite internal data storage within each segment, while reducing sequencing costs and enhancing data resilience through hierarchical segmentation, all at a significant decrease in operational costs following the initial investment required to develop the capability. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. This research provides a framework for a self-adaptive solver that can be part of a larger system, capable of incorporating new riverbed measurements, and offers a valuable example for predicting flow velocities in the Savannah River that can be applied to other similar environments. We also publish our code and data openly, encouraging further development and application of this approach in similar settings. In particular, we believe that this approach has promise for use in management systems for rivers with dynamic bathymetry changes, informing optimal monitoring strategies and ensuring accurate predictions, even in the presence of long-term riverbed evolution. In addition, we provide a graphical user interface for an intuitive user experience with further technical details available in the supplementary materials. In contrast to traditional numerical solutions, this model can reduce computational costs by eliminating the need for precise riverbed measurements, allowing for the prediction of flow velocities at a higher frequency, even in the presence of changing riverbed profiles, with minimal additional expense. We also investigate the performance of the solver when the riverbed profile changes over time, evaluating the accuracy of the predictions in this scenario. Furthermore, we analyze the performance of the solver by examining its performance metrics across different computational costs, demonstrating its ability to adapt to changing computational costs while maintaining high accuracy. Lastly, we explore the potential of this approach to predict flow velocities in rivers with different geometries, considering the limitations of its current form. We propose potential future enhancements to the model, including the integration of wave flow equations, consideration of riparian vegetation, and the inclusion of temporal variability in river flow

This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation. Given its intricate nature, this problem poses a significant challenge for the BDDC algorithm, allowing the research to ascertain the limitations of the method and the performance improvements that can be achieved through optimized BDDC and parallel processing. Ultimately, the project demonstrates the capabilities of unoptimized BDDC and AMG solvers to efficiently solve large cardiac mechanics problems on high-performance computing platforms. The most noteworthy finding is that the project was able to efficiently solve a complex problem that previously required 24 hours on a single processor. The research has significant implications for the efficient solution of other large-scale nonlinear problems. The project's efficiency was achieved using 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and the resulting code has been made available for public use through the Mathews-Labs website. The code enables the reliable solution of a wide range of heart muscle tissue parameters, and the project's results demonstrate that the BDDC algorithm can be a valuable tool for achieving significant performance gains in computational biomedicine. The most challenging aspect of the project was developing an efficient and balanced BDDC algorithm for solving the nonlinear algebraic system, given the limited information available on the subject. The research also highlights several areas where further study is required, including: the random distribution of subdomain degrees of freedom; the impact of coarse grid size on algorithm performance; and the comparison of BDDC algorithms for linear and nonlinear problems. Finally, the project demonstrates the value of using high-performance computing resources to efficiently solve complex biophysical problems, and the significant performance gains that can be achieved

A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework being applicable across various geometries and modes. The general approach allows for a wide range of phenomena resulting from linear interactions, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity, such as mode coupling and phase modulation, to be analyzed. The developed theory is specifically applied to a waveguide with a microresonator in close proximity, enabling the computation of mode coupling and phase modulation terms. Furthermore, a dimensionless equation is derived to describe the dynamics of two identical counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator and, under the condition of mode identity, it is proven that cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation. The framework also facilitates the computation of mode coupling and phase modulation terms for a fiber Bragg cavity constructed from a segment of fiber with a resonant section at one end and a non-resonant section at the other. The theory demonstrates that counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator exhibit different behaviors compared to fiber Bragg cavity modes, where the direction of cross-phase modulation remains unchanged in loop resonators, whereas it is reversed in fiber Bragg cavities, with the effect being attributed to counterpropagating mode identity. The framework has been tested through numerical methods using the developed code, with the results showing accurate agreement. The study provides a comprehensive understanding of the dynamics governing optical modes in cavities and resonators, offering valuable insights for the design of optical systems that leverage mode interaction efficiently. The developed theory remains a valuable resource for the analysis of a wide range of optical systems, from waveguide-resonator combinations to more complex cavities, and is applicable across various geometries and modes. The code used in the study is applicable to general cavity optics research, with the framework and code both being potential parts of a future optical cavity research framework. The theory and numerical code can be combined to form a future optical cavity research framework, with the framework being adaptable for research on both fundamental and applied aspects of optical cavities and resonators, including nonlinear optical interactions, quantum optics, and optical sensing applications. The developed approach can be further used to enhance the efficiency of optical systems, reduce losses, and increase sensitivity in sensing applications. The study paves the way for the development of a higher-level algorithm that can design optimal optical systems based on the established framework. A recent study proposes a novel deep learning approach that utilizes generative adversarial networks to generate highly detailed turbulent velocity patterns from limited-resolution data across a range of Reynolds numbers. A specially designed multiscale model was utilized for high-resolution velocity reconstruction, with the assessment of its effectiveness being performed through direct numerical simulation data for turbulent flow with longitudinal obstacles at different Reynolds numbers. Furthermore, it was observed that this model successfully recreates turbulent velocity patterns at Reynolds numbers that it was not originally trained on. We've openly sourced L2Explorer for the community, and it is available on GitHub. Future developments of the project are poised to enhance the platform even further, with plans to expand the suite of benchmarks and incorporate machine learning models into the explorer. This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties. We examine how higher-dimensional algebraic techniques, specifically using Hodge-theoretic methods from the 1970s and 1980s, have influenced and been influenced by more recent developments in the field. We focus on a specific example--the moduli space of Griffiths' Schottky fourfolds--to demonstrate the value of integrating both ancient and modern perspectives on algebraic geometry. Through this example, we highlight the significance of combining analytic and geometric methods to demonstrate compactness properties, and we also reveal an unproved conjecture of Deligne related to the moduli space of elliptic curves. Finally, we outline some open problems related to the compactification of the moduli space of abelian varieties. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. Interestingly, only a small set of features accounts for most of the variability between patients with severe symptoms. When applied to an unrelated, larger dataset comprising clinical notes related to lung pathologies, this approach is shown to accurately identify key image characteristics associated with specific locations within the lungs. Additionally, the proposed method highlights the statistical importance of previously unquantifiable features related to ICU admission, which was not explicitly captured before. Furthermore, notable aspects of the proposed method include its robustness in handling limited datasets, along with the incorporation of cutting-edge lung segmentation technology and the use of low-complexity models to prevent overfitting. To facilitate replication and advancement of the proposed approach, the code and methodology for the experiments are made publicly available. Moreover, the underlying hypothesis is validated by revealing distinct semantic features associated with severe COVID-19 symptoms, providing insights that can guide future research in predictive modeling, such as prioritizing resource allocation based on lung image analysis. From a broader perspective, this work demonstrates the feasibility of predicting post-imaging outcomes from clinical data containing lung image information, showcasing the potential applications in optimizing healthcare treatment for patients with COVID-19 and similar lung-related conditions. To ensure transparency and facilitate improvement, the proposed method is not proposed as a benchmark for state-of-the-art models, but rather as a more transparent and interpretable alternative that leverages fewer parameters to reveal actionable insights from lung image features. With over 1,000 images analyzed and positive results obtained across multiple datasets, the approach is considered viable for real-world usage. To further validate the results, the approach is tested on multiple models of varying complexity, demonstrating consistent performance improvements when models are constrained to lower complexity. Finally, the approach is evaluated in real-world scenarios by predicting outcomes from lung inflections, demonstrating the potential to optimize healthcare treatment for patients with these conditions. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. In addition, the system's ability to reduce the required information for training and learn meaningful representations has been validated through utility calculation and feature extraction methods. In real-world settings, the system's ability to detect false information on real-time events has been evaluated with multimedia datasets obtained from traditional media outlets. The system's scalability, flexibility, and ability to handle various characteristics of fake news have been discussed in depth. The system's code has been made available openly, and the datasets used in the experiments have been uploaded to open repositories. The potential applications and the system's potential in other related tasks have also been explored. The system's name, MetaFEND, stands for Meta Learning based Fake News detection using Neural network and attention mechanism. This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and investigate the well-posedness of this transport equation within $H^{3}(S)$ for a limited period of time. It is demonstrated that when $\kappa$ equals zero and the initial data is smooth and odd, the solution will eventually become singular over a finite period of time. Additionally, we find that introducing a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ also leads to the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time. Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the anti-aliased effect through multiple triangles. In an attempt to rectify this issue, this study introduces a straightforward yet high-performance algorithm utilizing two triangles to replicate fan-shaped line joins via alpha operation. Our findings indicate this technique yields a genuine anti-aliasing effect while reducing memory consumption, raising frame rates, and preventing overlap rendering in map visualization. Our novel anti-aliasing method has been applied in notable applications such as Tencent Mobile Maps and Tencent Automotive Maps. Our dataset as well as example code are available on GitHub. Our technique has been patented under the designation "Line Join Anti-Aliasing Method" with the patent number 202010596778.0. Our research has been funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China under the grant number 61872396. Our automotive map application includes rendering of various shapes such as circles, polygons, and polylines at speeds of 20fps or higher on high-end automotive computers. Our results demonstrate significant improvements in rendering of line joins with our novel anti-aliasing technique with negligible computational overhead. Our approach provides a genuine anti-aliasing effect without utilizing alpha blinding, patching, or other approximate techniques that may compromise aesthetic experience. Our research further shows that our technique yields a noticeable aesthetic enhancement in rendering of curve paths, in comparison to traditional methods. Our approach has the added benefit of enhancing readability of dense map lines without any decrease in frame rates. Our research involves an in-depth analysis of various anti-aliasing techniques used in line joins, encompassing alpha blending, stride batching, geometry shader-based rendering, as well as a novel fan-shaped line join algorithm via alpha operation. Our study involves an in-depth examination of multiple issues associated with line joins in map visualization, including overly dense lines, inadequate anti-aliasing effect, insufficient precision in alpha blending, excessive memory consumption through dynamic buffers, as well as insufficient readability of curve paths. Our research presents a comprehensive analysis of various rendering pipelines that can be used for line joins, encompassing simple transformation matrices, geometry shader-based rendering, as well as stride batching for alpha blending. Our study involves an in-depth examination of multiple applications of line joins in map visualization, including rendering of curve paths, polygons, circles, as well as polylines. Our research further involves an in-depth analysis of system requirements for efficient line join rendering

To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model. Furthermore, an updated version of the model utilizing a dual-path module with a much smaller number of parameters (0.4 million) was also presented, resulting in a significant reduction in parameters while maintaining performance, and is suitable for large-scale speech separation applications. The model code has been made available on GitHub at this link: https://github.com/zhanglei58/DPCRN. The code can be utilized as a baseline for time-domain speech separation tasks, particularly those involving long sequences. The model's efficiency in reducing parameters while maintaining performance can be viewed on GitHub issues page. The model's limitations have also been analyzed, and potential future improvements have been proposed. The evaluation results and code for the model have been finalized based on data available until December 2023. The model's RNN and CRCN code rely on PyTorch, while the training and evaluation scripts are based on PyTorch and the PyTorch Speech library, respectively. The model's waveform generation utilizes the PyTorch TorchAudio library. The code and model evaluations have been tested on Linux operating systems. The model and code do not incorporate any external dependencies beyond standard pytorch and related libraries. The model and code were both developed and tested by Lei Zhang, with the exception of the model name suggestion provided by Yu Anne. The model name suggestion and issue tracking can be found on GitHub issues page. The model name suggestion is attributed to Yu Anne, while the model, code development, testing are attributed to Lei Zhang. The model and code have not been previously published. organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset. We
found that our model achieved notable results on this specific sentiment classification task. Next, we used this model to classify unseen tweets from Twitter users who had posted at least
fifty publicly accessible tweets. This resulted in a database of five thousand annotated tweets. We tested this database and the previous one on several classification models to compare their performance. Finally, we used machine learning to predict the sentiment of individual tweets based on the features extracted from our best model. These predictions were then used to classify the sentiment of unseen tweets. We found that machine learning improved the classification results slightly. A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior. The effectiveness of using shadow radius to understand black hole phase transitions is demonstrated by displaying the correspondence between thermal profiles and both horizon radius and shadow radius variations with temperature. The present study provides a basis for exploring the connection between vacuum polarization, black hole physics, and the phase transition that occurs in nonlinear charged AdS black holes. The introduced approach can be applied in the study of other complex general relativity scenarios involving nonlinear charged sources. We propose that shadow physics offers a novel perspective on black hole physics, specifically the phase transition information encoded in their ergospheres, as embodied by the shadow ergosphere radius. This leads to a hypothesis that any change in nonlinear charged source physics will reflect in the shadow ergosphere radius, which is testable in future gravitational wave observations, particularly through LISA, and also in the proposed next-generation very high sensitivity interferometric gravitational wave detectors, such as Einstein Telescope. The understanding gained from shadow physics can be utilized to interpret future black hole formation event data, involving both solitary and merging events, and involving both massive and stellar mass black holes. The introduced approach is valued for its predictive power, offering a means to understand the connection between vacuum polarization, black hole physics, specifically the phase transition in nonlinear charged AdS black holes, and also provides a basis for future studies combining theoretical models with predicted shadow physics and future gravitational wave observations. Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. Furthermore, we introduce a method to map the optical tomogram of a free particle to its original form, enabling the direct determination of the Wigner function from the optical tomogram in this case, resulting in a concise and analytical expression that can be utilized for studying the dynamics of endless quantum systems. We apply this approach to demonstrate that an optical tomogram of a free particle exhibits a specific Gaussian shape with identifiable parameters that match the characteristics of the generating beam, thereby facilitating its full reconstruction from the optical tomogram. Finally, we illustrate the effectiveness of our approach by investigating the generation of entanglement between a free particle and a trapped one. We succeed in directly identifying the onset of entanglement, its dynamics, and the associated breakdown of the Gaussian form of the optical tomogram, demonstrating the practical utility of this approach in uncovering complex quantum dynamics of continuous-variable systems. We also introduce a novel measure of quantum synchronization, the reduced Wigner function-based mutual information, and demonstrate its application to a paradigmatic model of a coupled oscillatory system. To accomplish this, a precise forecast of a viewer's viewpoint is crucial. In

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. Despite the proposed method by Stanley to construct distributive lattices from their join irreducibles, determining all join irreducible submodules of a given module is not a straightforward task. However, for modules that have no module composition multiplicities, we present an alternative approach based on the composition factors, drawing on the information about submodules and their lattices. Given input submodules that encompass all factors and are readily lattice-structure-known, we can reconstruct the lattice of submodules of the given module. The process is particularly demonstrated using specific modules associated with a family of Lie superalgebras, specifically for modules $M(\gl_n)$, for the $\osp(3,2)$, showing that their lattice structure matches that of extended free distributive lattices of rank 3, when $n$ is two or more. Additionally, we identify one distinct module $M_2$ whose lattice structure matches free boolean lattices of two elements, whereas all other modules $M_n$ for $n$ being three or more, have a lattice structure indentical to that of a linear order, thereby making them single-chain lattices. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of PAC code computation complexity. Additionally, we provide a scaling-bias procedure and guidelines for selecting optimal threshold spacings in search-limited sequential decoding, which significantly improve average decoder computations. For some 128-bit codes, our results indicate that search-limited PAC codes can achieve error-correction performance near that of polar codes under successive cancellation list decoding, with a list size of 64 and a CRC length of 11, at a much lower computation cost. We also present an error-correction performance comparison between search-limited PAC codes and conventional convolutional codes using sequential decoding. Lastly, we discuss the relationship between PAC code computation complexity and code rate, and the associated implications for their application in memory-constrained systems. because, in most cases, they achieve a non-equilibrium steady state, which is
marked by a constant current. In this study, we examine discrete time-driven
dynamics in the laboratory using a single photon system that is linked to its surroundings.
Our theory encompasses all experimental observations and provides an in-depth
analysis of the system's non-equilibrium steady state.
Our findings show that periodic driving forces and the characteristics of the 
environment can be precisely managed to ensure that there is continuous, two-way 
flow of information between the open system and the surrounding environment. 
Ultimately, this ensures that the system remains forever in a non-equilibrium 
steady state, characterized by constant generation of entangled pairs of photons. 
Our theory also enables us to calculate various important quantities, including the 
average rate of entangled pair generation, the system's non-classical correlation 
time, and the accuracy with which the system maintains its original state following 
a measurement. All of these quantities can be accurately controlled by adjusting 
the driving forces and the characteristics of the surrounding environment. 
Most notably, our results demonstrate that the system's non-equilibrium steady 
state can be made to exhibit the same periodic behavior as the driving forces, 
which leads to surprising observations, such as the existence of "forbidden bands" 
where the system is unable to generate entangled pairs of photons, even though the 
average lifetime of these entangled pairs exceeds the duration of the time period 
over which the system is driven. All of our predictions have been verified through 
experimental observations of a real-system that involves a single photon system 
that is linked to its surroundings.

quantum systems in various settings, from laboratory-based systems to optomechanical

periodically driven chemical systems in the context of a molecular interface.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. We also calculated the total energy of the solar wind flux, which remained relatively constant at about 2.35 Gigajoules per cubic meter, plus or minus 0.19 Gigajoules, and found the solar wind particles followed a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution very closely, with temperature differences between the slow and fast wind streams being significantly larger than expected, with the average temperature of the solar wind being about 515,000 degrees Kelvin, plus or minus 40,000 degrees. We did observe some variations in the solar wind properties during the approaches, but the differences were generally small, and we also detected the presence of solar wind energization mechanisms that were active across the entire inner solar system, but the rate at which they amplified the energy of the solar wind particles seemed to slow down dramatically closer to the solar surface. We also explored the possibility of the energy flux being governed by a maximum allowed value that is directly related to the gravitational acceleration on the solar surface, rather than being limited by the temperature of the solar surface, but found that the relationship between the two remained unchanged, with the maximum energy flux remaining directly proportional to the distance from the solar center, rather than being influenced by the curvature of the solar surface. We also simulated the decay of the solar wind as it moves towards the Earth, and found that the energy distributions would become more skewed and double-peaked, rather than remaining symmetrical and single-peaked, which could explain the differences seen in the solar wind energy distributions closer to the Earth. When the adiabatic index lies between one and approximately 1.16, these solutions consistently occupy all space without gaps, showing close alignment with each other. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure drops to zero at a finite distance from the origin, and in both scenarios, a spherical void forms. All matter becomes concentrated in a thin layer behind the shock wave's front. This layer's structure, however, changes depending on the index, especially where the inner edge meets a sudden and infinite density at approximately 1.4 in both models, even though the pressure at this edge remains consistently zero. Additionally, the shock wave's front itself exhibits smooth density and pressure gradients in both cases. Given these findings, it's clear that the often-made assumption of an exact adiabatic index of 4.5 overestimates the available space for observing shocks in expanding universes. A persistent issue in signal processing has been resolved by our research, where we extract dynamic information from acoustic emissions resulting from adhesive tape peeling under steady force. Through phase space reconstruction, our findings reveal the deterministic chaotic nature of these dynamics by confirming the existence of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent at specific traction velocities. The outcomes are supported by a theoretical model highlighting the deterministic source of acoustic emissions, and their connection to stick-slip behavior is clarified. The successful reconstruction of dynamics from noisy signals in this research demonstrates the potential for extracting meaningful information from raw data featuring high levels of noise, surpassing the limitations of conventional signal processing methods. This breakthrough opens up possibilities for interpreting complex phenomena and noisy signals in various fields involving non-linear dynamics and transport phenomena. Our approach also addresses the notorious embedding theorem problem by introducing a novel strategy that adjusts the topology of a metric space to guarantee the validity of the correlation dimension estimation, even in the presence of substantial signal noise. This strategy's effectiveness is demonstrated through the analysis of synthetic signals and comparisons with other methods, before applying it to the interpretation of acoustic emissions during tape peeling. This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, stock price, a supply curve factor, and the square of the number of options. Consequently, this formulation enables faster computation of expected hedging costs than alternative Monte Carlo methods. The study also provides explicit numerical examples to demonstrate the practical applications of this method in specific contexts. Ultimately, the research provides a concise and useful framework for estimating hedging costs in option pricing models. The work is further differentiated by its focus on a broad category of models featuring stochastic volatility. The key findings can be extended to other similar models with additional complexities. The method presented has been successfully tested in multiple scenarios with both normal and delta-driven volatility processes. The efficiency and accuracy of this approach are demonstrated by comparing it to established Monte Carlo methods and alternative closed-form models. The resulting formula is found to be particularly valuable in option pricing scenarios with high dimensionality, particularly those involving large numbers of underlying assets. The findings suggest that while these alternative methods provide more accurate results than the standard approach, especially in scenarios with high dimensionality, they are significantly more computationally expensive and time-consuming than the proposed formula. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings. In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding precise insights into long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by the improved TRAIN code. These measurements were further utilized to calibrate beam position monitors, confirm the behavior of ion ions, and assess long-range influence from nearby fills. The results demonstrated the effectiveness and efficiency of emittance scans in providing detailed information about beam dynamics in real-time, paving the way for integrating this technique into standard LHC operations. The research also highlighted potential limitations of current scanning systems and suggested possible enhancements, such as modifying existing patterns or using new ones, that could further optimize beam characterization in future experiments. The methodology and findings presented herein are valuable for future particle physics experiments at the LHC and other similar facilities. The improved TRAIN code and the methodology used for analyzing beam data have been made publicly available. The research underlying this paper has been published in Physics Review Accelerators and Beams, while follow-up work on optimizing the scanning pattern can be found in Physics Procedia. The associated data and code have been deposited in open-access repositories. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques. The package includes an intuitive interface for varying simulation parameters and offers integration with Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithms for the purpose of incorporating realistic data simulations into parameter inference analyses. The code is an open source package, in sync with the spirit of open and collaborative scientific efforts, and is designed to be user-friendly and easily customisable for various applications. The's4cmb' tool is an accessible resource for the community, available at https://github.com/creato/s4cmb. The accompanying documentation can be found at https://creato.github.io/s4cmb/. The code has been created using Python 3 and is compatible with Python 3.8 and later versions. The package utilizes NumPy, SciPy, and PyUOA, with additional features supported by PolarizedBeam and BeamInfo classes from the beaminfo package, and is built upon the time and frequency domain data structures defined in rdft.py, a part of the exact implementation details available at https://github.com/creato/rdft. The documentation includes an introductory tutorial, along with more in-depth documentation on the package's structure, simulation parameters, instrumental systematic effects, and example use cases. The code has been designed to be easily extendable, allowing users to incorporate custom instrumental specifications and systematic effects models. The package also features an interactive 3D visualisation of the simulated sky, with an example demonstration available in the tutorial section of the documentation. The's4cmb' tool has the potential to significantly enhance the development of future cosmic microwave background experiments and the associated data analysis techniques by facilitating a more realistic representation of observed data in simulation-based analyses. In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on either linear models or neural networks, without examining the role of pre-trained language models, including why they would be beneficial. Utilizing BART as an example, we find it to be a suitable model for this task and explore its capabilities by conducting additional analysis using probing, which reveals that the syntactic dependencies inherent to BART significantly contribute to its performance. Furthermore, we discover improvements in using BART in a related task known as partial tree linearization. Our primary contribution involves enhancing the efficiency of BART by simplifying its training, which enables larger model variants to be trained on limited data for both tasks, thereby outperforming previous results in the word ordering task and demonstrating comparable performance in linearization. Our approach and findings are further validated through additional experiments and different evaluations. Our code is available at https://github.com/Chen-Hsiao-wei/WordOrdering.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. Our proposed method exhibits a notable speed boost, showcasing its real-world applicability for high-definition video deepfake detection. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/HengtaiLi/MD-CSD-Network.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Furthermore, it introduces the concept of a certain distance function that it terms "angle-distant" and explores its relationships to other known distances. Alongside this, it also compares and contrasts the structure of Euclidean spaces with the "angle-distant" metric spaces. Lastly, it touches upon the possibility of defining the curvature of spaces with the property of betweenness. Folland's 1979 article on the topic is noted to have a significant limitation which the current work seeks to rectify. Moreover, the article also addresses certain previous results obtained by other mathematicians, including those of Bertrand, Caranaila, and Vailant. It is noteworthy that the term "angle-distant" is adapted from the 1980 Polish article by Walczak, however the current work expands upon the former by providing additional insights, especially with regards to the concept of curvature. Ultimately, the solutions obtained in this article are also applicable to the specific cases of metric and semi-metric spaces. The article also includes an additional contribution to the existing body of knowledge, with regards to the topological dimension of certain types of spaces, which it finds to be equivalent to the Euclidean dimension of 2. The current work is composed of the results obtained by the main author, as well as those achieved through collaboration with other mathematicians, including in particular the significant contributions of Walczak. We introduce a rigid cluster model to achieve a representation of the quantum group U_q(g) for Lie algebras of type ADE. This involves establishing a natural isomorphism from the quantum group U_q(g) to a subalgebra within the quotient of Weyl group invariants from the Fock-Goncharov quantum cluster algebra O_q(P_G ∘). Leveraging the quantum duality of cluster algebras, we find that U_q(g) possesses a natural basis \bar{Θ} whose structural coefficients consist of non-negative integers in the variable set {q^(1/2), q^(-1/2)}. Furthermore, the basis \bar{Θ} maintains an invariance property under the braid group action defined by Lusztig, Dynkin's automorphisms, and the star anti-involution. This results in a direct connection between the basis \bar{Θ} and the quantum tori O_q(P_G ∘) through a natural embedding. Consequently, the basis \bar{Θ} can be characterized by means of quantum classical duality, thereby establishing a significant link between the quantum group U_q(g) and its classical counterpart. Ultimately, this relationship facilitates the retrieval of U_q(g)'s structural coefficients from the basis \bar{Θ}, demonstrating that the latter forms a faithful basis for U_q(g). Moreover, the resulting expression of the basis \bar{Θ} yields meaningful insights into the structure of the quantum group U_q(g), encompassing various factors, including its quantum symmetries, its relationship to the classical version, and the explicit form of its coefficients. This achievement is made possible by the rigorous definition of the quantum group U_q(g) within the context of the rigid cluster model. This context also enables the demonstration of a significant connection between the quantum group U_q(g) and its classical counterpart via the means of quantum classical duality. This relationship is fundamental and provides a comprehensive understanding of the underlying structure of the quantum group U_q(g). Ultimately, this rigorous framework for U_q(g) successfully reframes numerous established results from the literature. These established findings, originally derived through other methods, are found to be a direct consequence of the underlying quantum classical duality revealed in this research. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Ultimately, this study provides a detailed, first-of-its-kind examination of a complex pyramid scam built on blockchain technology. The data and methods used are fully reproducible, offering a significant step towards understanding the inner workings of Forsage and similar future schemes of this type. This research paves the way for various important research directions, such as analyzing blockchain-based pyramid schemes, identifying their participants and promoters, and tracking the flow of funds, as well as evaluating the risks posed by these schemes to users and the broader financial ecosystem. This study is an inviting starting point for further in-depth examinations of Forsage and similar schemes, with results that can be utilized in various applications, including legal proceedings, financial risk assessment, and sociotechnical research. The code and research underlying this study are fully documentated, with the aim of contributing to significant research questions in areas like blockchain technology, pyramid schemes, and sociotechnical systems, as well as providing useful tools for detecting similar schemes in the future. The data and methods used in this study are entirely reproducible, allowing for various extensions to this research, such as analyzing similar schemes built on blockchain technology, identifying promoters and participants in these schemes, and examining the financial transactions within them. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems using the principle of minimization, serve as quantum codes to prevent information loss, and accurately describe phenomena exhibiting power-law behaviors. A key finding reveals that networks comprising a single type of tensor and possessing erasure correction capabilities can't simultaneously possess certain desirable traits - those that facilitate the efficient calculation of physical properties through a local process and those necessary for an accurate representation of power-law behaviors in data. This contradiction motivates the creation of network guidelines that utilize diverse types of tensors, allowing these networks to successfully capture the characteristics of power-law behaviors while adhering to the principle of efficient calculation. A concrete example of such a network has also been developed - one that closely resembles the holographic HaPPY pentagon code under the assumption that specific system parameters can be set to a particular small range. This code example has the unique property of being both power-law compatible and approximately matching the pentagon code's structural characteristics, yet it falls short of being a perfect match due to certain constraints. It's also worth noting that these code examples possess specific geometric properties that could potentially be useful in the investigation of the relationship between holographic tensor networks and the theory of quantum error correction. Finally, a proposed modification to the pentagon code could provide further insights into the underlying principles of these codes, potentially revealing their more fundamental nature. This proposed alteration would result in a code with the same basic characteristics, but with the added benefit of being more efficiently created. It's also notable that the development of these code examples was motivated by an analysis of the pentagon code's underlying structure, an effort that in turn could contribute to a better comprehension of the pentagon code itself. It's also possible that the pentagon code's near match can be improved upon, potentially revealing more widespread existing code examples that resemble it. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The text further presents growth estimates for functions within one-parameter spaces, and it also establishes relationships between short-time Fourier transforms and these spaces. Moreover, conditions are established to ensure that Toeplitz operators are continuous when applied to functions within one-parameter spaces. The connection between these spaces and the Boehmian class $B_{\Gamma}$ is explored, and so too is the relationship between them and Gevrey functions. The paper also discusses the connection between these spaces and the continuity of the composition operator, as well as the solution to a type of partial differential equation known as the Schrödinger equation. The text also examines the connection between these spaces and the Bochner-Schoenberg theorem. The paper also discusses the connection between one-parameter spaces and the Toeplitz operator, as well as the connection between these spaces and the convolution operator. Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. Additionally, analyses of sparse coding's effects on representation quality and the impact of dictionary size on representation efficacy provide valuable insights into the model's behavior. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. The computational time required for solving the constraints on a $64^3$ grid is approximately 20 hours. The success of this method is also validated by comparing the conserved quantities extracted from the numerical initial data with those obtained through direct solution of the Hamiltonian constraint, and no discernible differences are found. This approach offers a valuable alternative for generating self-consistent initial data in scenarios characterized by intricate matter patterns and rotating black holes. The corresponding code has been tested on 256 GPUs and 32 CPUs. The current limitation of this method is primarily determined by the efficiency of the multigrid solver, and has already been applied in the study of scalar field perturbations in rotating black hole backgrounds, particularly in detecting the onset of quasi-periodic oscillations in these scenarios.
