As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical property when subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, allowing it to function under extremely high laser intensities. This component can modify the laser pulse polarization while simultaneously increasing the peak power, which has been demonstrated numerically with simulations. It shows that a high-intensity linearly polarized laser pulse can be converted to a higher-powered circularly polarized pulse. This conversion process achieves nearly complete efficiency, with about $98\%$ of the initial energy successfully converted. The required waveplate thickness was found to be inversely related to the electron density in the plasma and the strength of the magnetic field, which, for a specific plasma and field, was found to be approximately 1 cm. This type of plasma waveplate can serve a pivotal role in the effective deployment of multi-petawatt laser systems. It is also a promising component in applications involving laser-plasma interaction, particularly in the creation of highly inhomogeneous electron beams for radiotherapy devices. We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those of maximal rank. Moreover, this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half. Both of these decoding strategies are deterministic and provide guaranteed performance in the worst-case scenario. Our results also offer insights into the performance of list decoding of rank metric codes. Our work builds upon recent research by the same authors, where the original publications occurred in 2022 and 2023, respectively. We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 434 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. Using the ratio of [Ni~II] and [Fe~II] line strengths, we determined a nickel to iron abundance ratio 1.5 times the solar value. Progenitor mass estimates from nebular-phase and semi-analytical modelling placed SN~2020jfo's mass within the 12 to 15 solar mass range. Semi-analytical modelling also suggested the presence of a substantial hydrogen envelope in SN~2020jfo's progenitor, which is unlikely for Type II supernovae with short plateau phases. Nonetheless, we found one comparable example, SN~2018vo, with similar characteristics, and mapped the evolution of its possible progenitor using computational modelling. The results suggest that SN~2020jfo and SN~2018vo may have originated from super-giant progenitors with masses between 12 to 15 solar masses, and sizes around 100 to 150 solar radii, and distances from the centre of the Earth of approximately 5 to 6 solar radii. To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites. A possible application of this technology is the X-ray transient experiment satellite, scheduled to be launched in 2027, where it could reduce the sensor count by a factor of 9 while maintaining the same field of view. As a result, MuLE optics could potentially save the satellite 30 kg in weight and 15 W in power consumption. Moreover, this technology also offers considerable weight and power savings in ground-based LE instruments. Energetic particle detection was considered for MuLE, but it required additional segmentation that would decrease the field of view and increase the sensor count. Therefore, MuLE is particularly suited for space-based X-ray transient monitoring in astrophysical applications, but it is not considered suitable for particle physics research. A conceptual design for a satellite-based MuLE instrument has been created, along with an estimate of the required manufacturing precision and testing procedures. Although the muons passing through the sensor can cause dead time and some background noise, simulations indicate that this effect is minimal and the MuLE instrument can still detect X-rays with energies as low as ~0.1 keV. We establish a level set formulation for partial uniform ellipticity with symmetric concave functions, implying a viable strategy for studying second-order fully nonlinear elliptic and parabolic equations. This approach facilitates the extension of key results from the fully nonlinear context to equations satisfying partial uniform ellipticity. As an application, we derive Holder continuity for solutions to these equations. This research was motivated by the attempt to extend regularity theories for the Serrin type and boundary regularity for fully nonlinear elliptic equations. It is noteworthy that these results can be obtained independently of the partial uniform ellipticity condition. Nonetheless, in the process of proving solution regularity, we discovered the significance of partial uniform ellipticity, which is equivalent to a specific combination of convexity and concavity conditions on the driver operator, prompting us to develop its relevant theory. Ultimately, our findings represent a supplement to the regularity theories mentioned above. This research was initially intended to be a part of a broader project aimed at exploring the regularity of solutions to certain fully nonlinear equations, especially those described by the Mignot and Puel's model. It is also relevant to the study of second-order fully nonlinear parabolic equations with partial uniform ellipticity, for which Holder continuity of solutions can be established using the same methods used for the elliptic case. Consequently, these results are relatively standalone, whereas the regularity theories mentioned above require additional arguments involving time-dependent problems and the concavity condition is crucial for handling the gradient growth of the underlying operator. Hence, we are presenting these results as a distinct entity, although they were obtained within the context of a larger project focused on time-dependent problems. To investigate the structure of dark matter, a deep learning framework was implemented and used to explore the impact of velocity and density information on the formation of halos through $N$-body cosmological simulations. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a given point in time, in a specific range of masses. However, when testing the inclusion of velocity information with the standard model of cosmology, negligible improvements were found. By increasing the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations in the simulation, a significant improvement was observed in the halo mass prediction when adding velocity field information. Ultimately, when the simulation parameters were modified further, models trained on density information alone failed to predict halo masses accurately, demonstrating the importance of velocity field effects on the halo collapse, particularly in certain mass scales. Furthermore, when the simulation parameters were altered, significant improvements were observed in halo mass predictions when adding velocity field information, with variations directly correlated with the scalar perturbation amplitude. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models. These results demonstrate our approach's capability in handling a wide range of rotating star configurations, and highlight the benefits of using the Lagrangian framework in general relativistic applications. 

Furthermore, our results show that the differences between the Eulerian and Lagrangian approaches become more pronounced as the rotation velocity approaches the speed of light, and we have also investigated the effects of using different grid structures, as well as implementing the Comoving Coordinate Condition, on the equilibrium configurations obtained. This approach provides a versatile tool for integrating quasi-static evolution processes into rotating stars, and offers a promising framework for incorporating other forces, such as magnetic fields and binary interactions, into rotating stars. 

Finally, we have made the publicly available the software used in this research, along with an example dataset, at the address https://github.com/HiroN72/WR4NR. 

We close by outlining potential future directions for improving this approach, such as refining the root-finding algorithm, integrating the Comoving Coordinate Condition into the equations, and applying this method to binary star interactions. 

We have also calculated several known analytic solutions using our approach, including the stationary, spherically symmetric solution, as well as rotating stars under the conditions of uniform specific angular momentum and uniform density, matching the results obtained using the integral method.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the highest gain in model performance occurs in the early stages of labeling, with a significant increase observable even after just one hour of labeling. The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time detection required for multi-messenger astronomy. We highlight the method's substantial potential for future gravitational wave research and emphasize the necessity of vast datasets for effective deep learning applications. Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis shows that the primary factors contributing to decreased diversity included increased home isolation and lower willingness to explore new places, with altered visitation preferences exacerbating this decline in the long term. Consequently, this research implies that the pandemic may have long-lasting adverse impacts on the income diversity of urban settings, with resulting implications for managing public health policies in a way that balances strict measures with promoting diversity of urban encounters beyond the pandemic era. It also highlights the significance of investigating the interplay between physical and social interactions and urban diversity, as well as exploring policy interventions that foster resilience in this regard, as seen in the studied cities up to late 2021, although the rate of recovery varied across them.

Three-dimensional simulations of high-mass young stellar objects reveal that their surrounding disks break apart into multiple gravitationally bound objects. The accretion of these objects by the stellar body could explain the recently observed episodes of rapid growth. By post-processing a prior simulation using a one-dimensional model, researchers found that material accumulating at the inner disk does not always result in significant accretion bursts on its own. Rather, only the impact of high-density objects crossing a critical boundary can produce the observed effects. Key factors affecting accretion bursts include: the behavior of turbulent discs where objects can get stuck, as well as discs powered by magnetic winds that allow for bursts akin to those observed. Furthermore, interactions with thermal instabilities in the inner disk can influence the duration and intensity of bursts, while dense stars or migrating objects can produce different effects, such as mergers rather than bursts, and object disruptions that could result in super-Eddington outflows affecting their surroundings. Consequently, details of high-mass YSOs' evolution can be complex and varied, offering possible explanations for recently observed phenomena, and highlighting their potential for powerful accretion episodes. Additionally, interactions with turbulent discs can lead to persistent accretion patterns, and magnetic discs can exhibit bursts that may match those seen in X-rays, although more realistic models are necessary for final confirmation. Ultimately, the behaviour of high-mass YSOs' inner regions can be sensitive to their outer regions' properties, thereby requiring comprehensive simulations that consider both areas. This research investigates how a uniform shear flow influences the behavior of water waves in an infinite, two-dimensional domain, specifically those with nonzero constant vorticity. We sought to analyze how a uniform shear flow affects weakly nonlinear, surface gravity waves through the use of Hamiltonian formulation and Hamiltonian transformation techniques. By applying these methods, we obtained a new Hamiltonian Dysthe equation describing the time-dependent evolution of the wave envelope. Our study confirms previous findings, revealing that the direction and intensity of the shear flow either strengthen or weaken the modulational instability of waves, depending on their characteristics. Our approach also facilitates a non-perturbative approach to determining the water's surface elevation, leveraging the Birkhoff normal form transformation to eliminate irrelevant triadic interactions. We validated our model against both direct numerical simulations of the full Euler equations and a comparable Dysthe equation proposed by Curtis, Carter, and Kalisch, discovering that it accurately replicates their results across various levels of vorticity. Our study demonstrates that the Hamiltonian Dysthe equation effectively captures the dynamics of water waves in shear flow, even in the presence of strong vorticity. Furthermore, we discovered that the Hamiltonian Dysthe equation exhibits an Hamiltonian-Hamiltonian structure, which facilitates the derivation of a rigorous energy inequality, thus ensuring the well-posedness of the equation and the conservation of both energy and action over time. This research paves the way for exploring the effects of arbitrary vorticity on water waves through the use of Hamiltonian formulation and Hamiltonian transformation techniques, as well as providing a suitable model for examining wave behavior in infinite domains with nonzero constant vorticity. It also offers a relevant model for investigating the effects of arbitrary vorticity on water waves in domains without constant vorticity, facilitating further study of this complex phenomenon. It ultimately aims to contribute to the comprehensive understanding of the Hamiltonian formulation of Hamiltonian equations with Hamiltonian transformation structure, which was initially explored by its authors through a relevant example. It also seeks to provide a suitable model for examining wave behavior in infinite domains with arbitrary vorticity, facilitating further study of this complex phenomenon. Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination, within a layered control framework. Capable of operating in harsh environments, the sonar sensors are positionally versatile on the robot, facilitating optimal navigational results through a zoning system. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model, along with a designed controller structure. Both theoretical simulation and practical testing on a mobile robot in an office environment, with real-time 2D navigation using one to three sonar sensors, are presented. Diverse sensor configurations were successfully implemented to validate the modularity of the system. Experimental results show that this method yields stable and secure indoor navigation in the presence of moving objects. A demonstration of outdoor riverbank navigation using a single moving sonar sensor is also provided, showcasing the adaptability of this approach. To support and validate the methodology, both artificial and real-world data were used in numerical experiments to illustrate the algorithm's performance. Interestingly, our approach can be viewed as an iterative version of the recently introduced dual certificate method, providing an alternative perspective on this technique. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels by examining the classification of utterances with the same annotation as mutual paraphrases. We demonstrate this approach to be a reliable means of evaluating and revising the annotations of intricate textual data sets containing complex semantic labels. Furthermore, we employ this evaluation method to rectify existing annotations of the EMO20Q dataset, thereby creating an updated version called EMO20Q-BERT. This revised dataset is found to exhibit decreased annotation noise levels. We also investigate aspects of dialog behavior that BERT struggles to differentiate based on textual context alone. Ultimately, our work highlights the value of pre-trained natural language models in the annotation process itself, enabling the refinement of existing annotations and the creation of more accurate annotated data sets. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use. 

With HiTMap, a notable improvement in navigation performance was observed, and the representation showed promise in facilitating independent navigation in unfamiliar environments. However, possible limitations of the system, such as its difficulty in retaining memory of previously explored areas and its limited ability to differentiate between various types of frontiers, also became apparent. Ultimately, HiTMap is presented as a modular framework that enables further development and customization of the system. The code for HiTMap is being continuously refined and is openly accessible on GitHub, inviting feedback and future collaboration.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla. This study demonstrates the feasibility of this novel approach by mapping the expelled local magnetic field strengths from a high-temperature superconducting plate in relation to the position of atoms in a Mach-Zehnder interferometry setup, and has shown that such measurements can be made with precisions comparable to those achieved through magnetic field isolation chambers. As a result, this research reveals the Meissner effect's potential to generate strong local magnetic fields that can be accurately measured, and also sheds light on the expulsion mechanism itself by mapping the expelled field's spatial distribution with atomic interferometry. This has implications for ranking superconducting materials according to their expelled field strengths. Furthermore, using the developed model, this study estimates the expelled local magnetic field strengths from bulk superconductors at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla. This achievement is made possible by employing atomic measurements in conjunction with numerical simulations of the Meissner effect. This combines physical insights into the superconducting phenomenon with the accuracy provided by atomic measurements. This approach also presents a novel application of atomic interferometry that expands its measurement capabilities to include magnetic fields generated by the Meissner effect, a phenomenon with direct connection to fundamental superconducting properties. This research was conducted in a low-vacuum environment to minimize residual gas interaction with the superconducting material, and employed a design where the superconducting plate and atoms are positioned in a way that expels the measurement of residual gas interactions with the superconducting material from the setup. This enabled the achievement of precise measurements of the expelled local magnetic field strengths from the superconducting plate, and demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach by employing a natural abundance $^{12}$C isotope-enriched diamond as a substitute for the superconducting plate in a parallel experiment. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  The framework and related research are further illustrated through various examples and graphical visualizations in the additional files listed below.  These files also contain the DynaSOAr framework itself, the CUDA driver integration, the CUDA test suite, the stream compiler modifications, the GCC compiler modifications, the new memory allocator implementation, the memory layout DSL, the do-all operation implementation, the benchmark results, and the presentation slides.  Our DynaSOAr framework has been openly available since 2009 at the address [www.cs.umbc.edu/~ostehlik/research/dynasoar].  It remains an active, production-ready project with ongoing support and updates. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties.  Our study suggests that nitrogen-rich environments could result in both carbon and nitrogen defects, whereas oxygen-rich environments would likely lead to the formation of O-O bonds with defect magenetism as seen in previous research, rather than magnetic defects from substitutional sites.  Consequently, to confidently predict the magnetic properties of doped TiO2, it is essential to consider the composition of the used source gas thoroughly.  Ultimately, this study demonstrates that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects are responsible for the magnetic properties observed in TiO2, rather than surface defects formed through aging, as previously proposed.  Furthermore, we propose that modifying TiO2 by introducing defects could result in damping of spin flip Raman scattering, and thereby enable the direct observation of defect induced magnetism in bulk TiO2.  Our predictions are compatible with experimental findings from Raman and XPS measurements, and could be tested in future experiments utilizing deeper characterization techniques.  Ultimately, this study reinforces the idea that TiO2 possesses unique and versatile properties, making it a promising and multifaceted research subject. This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ which would significantly surpass the current world records, with limits on branching ratios of $<0.39\cdot10^{-5}$ and $<0.97\cdot10^{-5}$, respectively. Finally, I show that the elastic process remains too elusive to be worthwhile analyzing, but the semi-elastic process offers considerable potential for improving the current limits on rare decays like $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ by a factor of ten or more. Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that such groups cannot be constructed as infinite, simple groups and that only finite groups with a polynomial diameter are identified, including cyclic and solvable groups, as well as a class of non-solvable groups known as classical Coxeter groups. Additionally, it is shown that the largest possible abelian section's index increases significantly with decreasing diameter, implying that diameter indices polynomial growth are characterized by having a large abelian section close to the group's highest order. This research also explores the relationships between groups with a diameter that scales polynomially and other important properties, such as finite groups' potential for multiple conjugacy classes, large nilpotent subgroups, simple group non- existence, and specific subgroup structures. It is noted that the concepts developed here can be applied more broadly to other infinite group types, including countable Coxeter groups, automorphism groups of trees, and branch groups. It is also observed that finite groups with a polynomial diameter are relatively rare, consisting of a few established examples, and it is proposed that the study of these groups may be valuable in the future. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C. The temperature sensor module was integrated into a voltage and frequency scaling system, demonstrating a significant reduction in average power consumption of up to 20% in real-world applications. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.  Ultimately, it is crucial to thoroughly investigate the characteristics of high-mass protostellar cores and the conditions necessary for their formation.  This knowledge will not only help us understand the formation of high-mass stars but also aid in identifying suitable targets for future high-resolution spectroscopic studies of embedded massive star-forming regions.  By doing so, we can better comprehend the evolutionary paths that massive star-forming cores and prestellar cores follow.  This knowledge will be crucial for developing criteria for finding massive star-forming cores that are actively producing gamma-rays, particularly those capable of producing high energies necessary for producing cosmic rays. Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness. The constructed operators take the form of reciprocal functions, with singularities handled through the application of the Pizzetti formula. The utility of these operators is illustrated through the example of obtaining positive definite functions on spaces of higher dimensions, starting from a given reference system. The relationship between these operators and the conventional methods of differentiation and integration is also explored, along with the rule governing their composition. The connection between these operators, the Pizzetti formula, and the reciprocal function is demonstrated, along with the possibility of extending them to a broader class of functions. The paper concludes by introducing the concept of pseudo-reciprocal functions, which can be used to extend the properties of the constructed operators to other, more general contexts. The utility of these operators is shown to extend beyond the realm of geometry, also being applicable in any situation characterized by a system of special functions, typically defined through a recursive relationship involving differentiation and integration. The paper further establishes the link between these operators and the Pizzetti formula, revealing that the formula itself can be viewed as a kind of pseudo-reciprocal function. The paper's contributions are threefold. Firstly, it demonstrates the feasibility of altering the dimension of a system of special functions, while ensuring the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness. Secondly, it presents the underlying operational relationship among the operators, the Pizzetti formula, and the associated reciprocal functions. Lastly, the paper reveals the general applicability of these operators, which can be utilized in any context featuring a system of special functions defined through a recursive relationship involving differentiation and integration. The paper's findings have implications for the application of conventional methods of differentiation and integration in geometry, as well as in other contexts characterized by a system of special functions. The paper further shows that the constructed operators can be extended to a broader class of functions

Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. The validity of our "leverage rule" has been confirmed through an alternate approach based on curvature effects. The resulting model has been successfully applied to predict stress values during motion and to evaluate the likelihood of the stick-slip or stationary regimes. The integration of the "leverage rule" into the roughness factor allows for a distinct classification of the stick-slip regime into two sub-categories, thereby providing insights into the behavior of dry liquid foams during motion. The significance of the curvature of Plateau borders in determining the likelihood of the stick-slip or stationary regimes has been confirmed by the application of our model to a variety of rough surfaces, including natural rocks and artificial surfaces with controlled textures. The important role of curvature in the behavior of dry liquid foams during motion has implications for the interpretation of previous studies, which did not account for this factor, and highlights the necessity of considering the curvature of Plateau borders in the evaluation of the stick-slip or stationary regimes. This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective. Furthermore, our results suggest that the anomaly class might be related to the condition known as vitiligo. Our code and dataset annotations are available for public use at our repository.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, is examined in a study that also compares its inextensibility to that of an extremely elastic membrane. When the inner fluid density surpasses the outer fluid density, the membrane exhibits a Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability caused by centrifugal force, competing with the curvature and tension-driven restorative forces, thus dictating the size of the developed finger. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. In particular, the look-ahead attention mechanism yields a significant 8.1% increase in translation accuracy for the NIST Chinese-to-English task when using the strong LSTM baseline, and also achieves notable gains on other translation tasks with different baselines. In addition, we visualize target word dependencies through look-ahead attention graphs, and the resulting plots are found to be highly consistent with existing linguistic analyses. In summary, this paper presents a novel attention model component, demonstrates the importance of target word dependencies in translation, and shows the wide applicability and efficiency of look-ahead attention across various translation tasks and baselines. The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on applying research directly. In the process, we highlight valuable insights that can be applied to other projects in the field of translational computer science. Further, we outline the lessons learned from grid computing development, including its successful deployment, applications in various fields, and notable achievements, such as its use in large scientific projects and as an underlying infrastructure for other initiatives. Finally, we highlight potential opportunities and challenges in grid computing, showing how it has been adopted in various forms around the world, but also faces ongoing technical difficulties and resource requirements. We believe that the successful development of grid computing provides a viable model for other projects in the field of translational computer science. We hope that by using grid computing as an example, we can encourage more research in translational computer science, demonstrating the value of applying computing research directly and efficiently. We also emphasize the potential benefits of this approach for computing research itself, pointing out how applying research directly can accelerate the process, decrease costs, and result in more reliable technology. Consequently, we propose increasing the focus on applying research directly, incorporating feedback from users and real-world applications into the development process, and prioritizing the simplest possible implementation of innovative ideas, as well as publishing detailed instructions for others to reproduce and build upon existing research and projects. We outline the potential benefits and challenges of this approach, present possible scenarios for applying research directly in various computing fields, and provide practical advice for doing so, along with empirical evidence from successful projects that have thrived as a result of a focus on applying research directly. We also outline potential opportunities and challenges in grid computing, showing how it has been adopted in various forms around the world, but also faces ongoing technical difficulties and resource requirements. We believe that the successful development of grid computing provides a viable model for other projects in the field of translational computer science. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude. Our research demonstrates that J/ψ invisible decays offer promising insights into light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter, particularly for regions of their parameter spaces that direct detection and other experiments may not cover. Our study suggests that further investigation into the properties of these particles is necessary and that J/ψ invisible decays can be an important component of future dark matter and neutrino searches at colliders. The various effective operators and their associated energy scales also provide useful benchmarks for future searches and could be easily extended to include additional interactions with quarks and photons. The parameter $\phi(x,b)$ is determined by the probability $\mathbb{P}(\text{L\'evy}(1/2,\kappa(x,b))<0)$ where $\kappa(x,b) = \frac{\sqrt{1-x}b-\sqrt{1+x}}{\sqrt{1-x}b+\sqrt{1+x}}$ with $b = b_S \geq 0$ indicating the relative magnitude between positive and negative excursions of the random walk. The condition $b \geq 0$ represents a boundary that distinguishes the behavior of walks with more significant positive than negative excursions from those with more significant negative than positive excursions, demonstrating a sharp transition in probability distributions. The resulting formula implies that the probability of the random walk spending the majority of its time within the non-negative region decreases rapidly as time progresses, with the rate of decay dictated by the probability of a corresponding L\'evy variable taking on non-negative values. The power law decay also extends to random walks that have zero mean but have increments that follow a common power law distribution with parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$, in contrast to the traditional parabolic behavior seen in the central limit theorem. The resulting formula provides a clear indication of the impact of the power law nature of the distribution on the random walk's behavior, revealing a significant shift from the effects seen on smaller time scales, with the power law decay rate being significantly increased beyond the square root of time, consistent with observations seen in real-world data scenarios. The research further reveals the power law decay's dependence on the parameter $\beta$, which measures the disparity between positive and negative excursions, with the probability distribution being essentially unchanged for a period of time prior to becoming significantly asymmetric, indicating that the power law nature of the random walk's behavior is remarkably robust across different time scales. The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and to optimize the source for maximum plasma density, it was modified to function in this mode at the highest magnetic field available. This involved increasing the diameter of the plasma chamber from 0.4 to 0.8 meter, which also improved particle power balance, but required additional power to function. It was found that in helicon mode, a layer of dense plasma forms near the center of the chamber, but it is limited by a edge plasma barrier, and increasing the diameter chamber helps to overcome this limitation. It was also discovered that to achieve helicon mode, the position of the magnetic field center needs to be adjusted, which can be challenging, but it was achieved in the modified source, which has a higher plasma density suitable for the IShTAR experiment. It was also found that in helicon mode, there are areas near the chamber walls where plasma density is very low, and it was confirmed that increasing the diameter chamber helps to reduce this plasma inhomogeneity, and it was estimated that with the modified source, it would be possible to achieve a plasma density of 4 x 10 to the power 10 unit per cubic meter at 3.5 MHz frequency. It was also found that in helicon mode, there are areas near the chamber walls where plasma density is very low, and it was confirmed that increasing the diameter chamber helps to reduce this plasma inhomogeneity. It was also estimated that with the modified source, it would be possible to achieve a plasma density of 4 x 10 to the power 10 unit per cubic meter at 3.5 MHz frequency. It was also found that in order to achieve a higher plasma density, it would be necessary to use a different type of antenna, which would allow plasma density to increase to 10 x 10 to the power 10 unit per cubic meter.

While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. Additionally, this approach provides a feasible solution for automatically detecting and counting certain cell features from large images by using a region-of-interest (ROI)-based strategy. Experimentation with real-world datasets shows that this approach delivers notable gains in performance, surpassing existing models in several metrics. Furthermore, the simplicity of this approach makes it highly efficient, requiring significantly less computational resources than other state-of-the-art models. In evaluation experiments with real-world cancer datasets, this approach demonstrates its capability to extract valuable information from large images with minimal manual intervention. The code for this research is available on GitHub at the address specified in the text. The author hopes that this approach and the associated code will be useful to other researchers and practitioners in the field of computer vision and pathology image analysis. The text also includes a code tutorial for reproducing the results presented in the evaluation experiments. The approach presented in this research has the potential to be expanded for use in other tasks that involve the automatic detection of specific objects within large images. The text includes a discussion of these possibilities and the potential challenges associated with them. The approach provided in this paper has been tested and validated through various experiments described in the text. Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. A study on sending handwritten digits to a GCNN as input reveals revealing patterns of contribution from various feature combinations, offering tangible evidence of the non-linear elements' ability to capture complex, collective patterns of input data. This comprehensive study of GCNNs' underlying mechanics provides a solid foundation for further research and potential applications, giving readers a thorough understanding of how GCNNs function and why they are valuable tools. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our approach is called the "separated agent method" and our code
is available for public use. Our research demonstrates the critical importance
of dynamics model structure in multi-task settings and highlights potential
applications for our approach in other learning scenarios involving shared
representations. Our simplest implementation is particularly effective at
generalizing to unseen tasks with minimal parameter expenses, making it an
attractive solution for discovering optimal model architecture across multiple
tasks. Our approach can be viewed as a form of network snipping that not only
improves performance but also provides actionable insights into the underlying
dynamics of each task by revealing sub-networks associated with each individual
task. Our separate agent method has a direct analogy with established best
practices for handling concurrent behaviors in physics-based models, such as
graph-based separation of object affiliations, which we term "object snipping".

in multi-task settings and reveals sub-networks associated with each individual
task, making it a valuable tool for understanding the underlying physics of

This work demonstrates that the essential conclusions of these theorems can be derived from a single key result, which in turn is deducible from a minimal axiomatic foundation consisting of a tiny formal system with the ability to perform limited mathematical operations and reasoning. This formal system, which we'll refer to as "Minimal", is notable for its significantly reduced set of axioms and rules when compared to standard formal systems used in mathematics, and serves as a significant distortion of conventional formal systems. As we distend the "Minimal" system to create more comprehensive and realistic formal systems, we can find connections to prominent results in the field of mathematical logic. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. Additionally, our method includes a mechanism to ensure positivity of the produced images, which is crucial in certain inverse problems involving compressive sensing. When combined with coarse initializations, our approach is capable of real-time sampling from highly complex posterior distributions with realistic results. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/yangyi1993/WASPGAN. Moreover, we launched a web-based demo at http://waspgan.csail.mit.edu/, which allows users to upload their own images and try out our method. Our approach has the potential to be used in real-time medical imaging procedures, which are typically slow due to the computational requirements of current sampling methods. This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. These discussions highlight the significance of invariant sets in dynamical systems, demonstrating how their preservation is crucial for maintaining system properties and solutions' stability. In this context, we emphasize the critical role that invariant sets play in maintaining a system's desired behavior and its impact on the solutions' stability. This is particularly evident when we consider the consequences of a system losing its invariant sets, as this can lead to the system exhibiting more complex behavior, including the creation of periodic orbits, the emergence of novel dynamics, and even the development of bifurcations. This knowledge can be utilized to determine the conditions under which a system will maintain its current dynamics or switch to a different dynamic state. This understanding is not only vital for predicting a system's future behavior but also for identifying suitable control strategies that can be employed to influence the system's dynamics. This is particularly apparent when we consider real-world applications such as the stabilization of chemical reactions, the control of neural networks, and the management of population dynamics. In these contexts, the loss of invariant sets can result in undesirable outcomes, including the degradation of the system's performance, the disruption of its stability, or even its complete failure. Consequently, it is essential to monitor the system's invariant sets closely to ensure that they remain intact and continue to benefit from the desirable dynamics and properties they provide. This knowledge can be utilized to make informed decisions about when to intervene in the system to prevent the loss of its invariant sets, which in turn will protect the system from the negative consequences of its dynamics changing over time. This is particularly evident when we consider the consequences of a system gaining new invariant sets as it undergoes changes in its dynamics. In this context, the emergence of novel invariant sets can be associated with the birth of new solutions, while the disappearance of existing ones is linked to the death of others. This information can be used to predict how the system's solutions will evolve over time, which in turn will influence our understanding of the system's future behavior. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. This screen's small size, 0.54 parsecs in diameter, suggests it is likely a solid cloud rather than a sheet-like structure like Eridanus Blob 1. Another screen, located about 8.57 parsecs from the Earth, is associated with a larger structure, Eridanus Blob 1, which has been previously identified, and exhibits distinct seasonal variations in scintillation intensity, indicating the screen's orientation and its effects on the surrounding gas. The observation of this screen over three and a half decades has revealed a notable increase in scintillation amplitude on the Earth's side of the orbit, likely caused by a directed gas flow within the blob, supported by additional data from the Pulsar Exploration Array. The detection of these screens and their dynamics in the interstellar medium is a significant advancement in understanding the medium's small-scale structures and their effects on the surrounding environment. The method used in this analysis provides a useful tool for analyzing future pulsar scintillation data, which will be essential for understanding the complex evolution of the interstellar medium. The data from this study will also be useful for modeling the propagation of ultra-high energy particles, such as neutrinos and cosmic rays, which are affected by the same screens in the line of sight to the Earth. The most distal screen, located about 13 parsecs from the Earth, exhibits the most rapid transverse motion ever observed in an interstellar screen, with a velocity component of 14.1 km/s, making it the most distant known scintillation source associated with a linear feature in the interstellar medium. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Additionally, QPNet's performance is compared to alternative WN pitch control methods, showcasing its superiority in low-frequency synthesis and its applicability to non-speech quasi-periodic signals like guitar audio. The proposed model provides a versatile framework for high-fidelity generation of various quasi-periodic signals with extended frequency ranges. The code for QPNet is available at https://github.com/author/QPNet.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Additionally, this framework facilitates the extension of universal properties from functors associated with THH to those associated with Berman's extension of THH, thereby yielding shadow representations of universal properties that possess greater generality. Moreover, it is shown that functors from the THH of a category are equivalent to shadows of that category, thereby providing a more abstract, bicategorical explanation for the relationship between functors from the THH of a category and its algebraic shadow. Lastly, it is proven that the algebraic shadow of a category is uniquely defined, resolving a previous conjecture, whereas the category shadow of a bicategory possesses a more elevated degree of nonuniqueness, arising from the inherent properties of Morita equivalence. Consequently, this theory provides a robust, axiomatic extension of the characteristics shared by THH, ultimately demonstrating its fundamental invariance under extensions to bicategories. Ultimately, this framework offers a novel, axiomatic understanding of the properties and characteristics of THH, thereby establishing its enduring significance within the theoretical context of category theory and homotopical algebra. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. Our sound source localization algorithm has been open-sourced on GitHub.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. Additionally, LGCN achieves comparable performance to GCNs in Euclidean geometry but with significant parameter reductions, demonstrating its scalable architecture. We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context. Furthermore, our exponential model can be applied to calculate
expected costs resulting from delay-driven decisions, offering a practical
application. We also conduct a statistical analysis of the Tsallis distribution in
relation to delay discounting, which follows a non-extensive probability
distribution. This study offers a straightforward approach for examining the
Tsallis distribution in societal settings and provides a practical exemplification
of its utilization in economic decision-making. Human participants' data from a
previous study are utilized as an example of the model's implementation. The
results of our research reveal a significant connection between the Tsallis
distribution's non-extensive nature and delay discounting's hyperbolic behavior,
which has been observed in various cultures worldwide. We propose that the
Tsallis distribution's parameters can serve as a cultural indicator, similar to
other standardized metrics, and provide a future research agenda on the topic. We also outline the advantages and limitations of using the Tsallis delay
discounting model, which is an original exponential model featuring a dual
nature, and offer the code for calculating delay discounting parameters from any
distribution of delay discounting. The code is available at https://github.com/
yamahisuematsu/Tsallis_DDD. We conclude by emphasizing the potential of the
Tsallis delay discounting model to accommodate various distributions of delay
discounting, and encourage researchers to apply the model in cultural settings.
We also examine the cultural invariance of the model's parameters in different
populations, and suggest that delay discounting's hyperbolic behavior is a
worldwide phenomenon with specific parameters that are influenced by culture.

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.  The resulting action is invariant under the appropriate group of harmonic gauge transformations, a syndrome of non-Abelian gauge symmetry that is an additional feature of this approach.  The impact of the massive gravity self-energy is explicitly shown to be negative, in agreement with previous findings, and the approach can be readily extended to the full linearized theory comprising a gravitational field and a massive scalar field.  The formalism also implicitly includes the linearized version of the dRGT massive gravity theory, which the approach is based on, as a natural component of the fundamental harmonic gauge theory.  The effect of the massive gravity self-energy on the Compton scattering amplitude is subsequently calculated and shown to lead to a negative contribution to the scattering cross-section.  This effect becomes more pronounced with increasing energy, due to the impact of the massive gravity self-energy on the energy shift of the Compton scattering process, which could be tested in future experiments with high-energy Compton scattering off nuclei, where the large number of collisions would make the effect more evident due to the larger number of Compton scatterings off individual nucleons.
